Τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πόνου, καὶ δὲ πυρώδης ἂν ὅσον ἐγκρατῇ, καίτοι φύσει ἀνωφερῆ ὄντα, ὅμως πειθόμενα τῇ τῆς ὅλου Διὸς πίξει, ἐγκρατῆται οὐ τοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ συγγείματος. καὶ δὲ γεώδη δὲ τὸ οὖ σοι ἂν, ἡ δὲ ὑγρόν, ἡ τὰ κατωφερῆ ὄντα, ὅμως ἐμένειν ἢ ἔνωσις τὴν ὀχ ἔχων φυσικὴν σάσιν. ὅταν οὖν ἡ τὰ τοιχεῖα ὑπακοῦ εἰς ὅλους, ἐπειδὰν π̣ς καταλαχθῇ σωὶ βία μένοντα, μέχρις ἂν ἐκεῖθεν πάλιν δι᾽ ἀνύσιμον τῆς διαλύσεως σημεῖον. ὁ δὲ ψυχὴν ἓν μόνον τὸ νοοῦν σε μέρος ἀπειθὲς ἔν, ἡ ἀγανακτεῖν τῇ ἑαυτοῦ χώρᾳ. Τὸ δὲ ὅσοι γε βίαιον τοῦτο ὑπὸ πάσῃ· ἀλλὰ μόνα, ᾧ φύσιν ἐστὶν αὐτῷ. οὐ μὲν τοι ἀνέχεται, ἀλλὰ τῶν ἐναντίαν φέρεται. ἢ ἢ ὑπὸ τὰ ἀ-
units.tr: "Will someone despise me? Let him see to that. But I will take care not to show myself worthy of contempt. Will he hate me? Let him see to that. But I will be gentle and kind to everyone, and ready to show even him where he is mistaken, not in a spirit of reproach or as one enduring hardship, but openly and kindly, as Phocion did, unless he was speaking in irony. For the inner self must be such that no one can hurt it, and a man who is not injured does not feel himself hurt. What harm is there in doing what is natural to man? Man is made for doing good to his fellows, and for bearing with them: as the feet, the hands and the eyes were made for working together, so men were made to act together, not to oppose one another. To set oneself against nature is to do wrong. Why do these people act as they do? Because they must busy themselves with public affairs, and you should not be angry with them but teach them. [illegible] Reason fails only when a man is mistaken about what is good for him. Men who go wrong do so because they do not know the truth, and once they learn it they will stop. Be cheerful, then, for life is short, and as the great ruler of the universe has ordered things, you should accept your lot. Consider the origin of all things, how they are composed of elements and change, and how no evil has befallen them. Remember also that we were made for one another, and that nature governs the whole. Some men are disagreeable at table, and act with a kind of pride, as though they were under compulsion; but if they act rightly you should not be vexed, and if they act wrongly, they do so out of ignorance, for no soul is willingly deprived of the truth. Men are angry when they hear what is right, and are unjust, unkind and grasping, and like those who sin against their neighbour. Consider first that you too often do wrong yourself; then that a fault of this kind may be excused by ignorance, or by some necessity, or by a habit of mind not wholly under one's control. Second, consider that those who sin are sometimes led astray by their own judgment. Third, that when you are very angry, life is short and all things soon pass away. Fourth, that the deeds of others are not in our power but in theirs; and that to think them dishonourable is a judgment of the mind, which may be removed. Fifth, that anger does not come from injury but from our own opinion of it, and that we can set it aside by reasoning, since it is not shameful and not a true evil. If a man is hurt, it is by his own hand, and if he is angry he will do more wrong than the one who wronged him. Sixth, that the harm one does in anger is often greater than the injury received. Seventh, that the anger of a wise man is not violent but gentle, and that it is better to bear wrong patiently than to strike back. Eighth, that anger and grief are weaker than reason, and that a calm mind is stronger than either. Ninth, that what the man who has insulted you intends is his own affair; be gentle, and show him that you are not moved. Do not hurt him, for that is what you would do to yourself, and it is unworthy of a man. Keep this principle in mind always: that men are born to act justly, and so long as you live, treat them as men. Guard against anger, and guard equally against flattery, for both are harmful. Be gentle, for that is more human and more manly; and when you have learned to be calm, you will be stronger than the angry man. Let your mind, which is the guiding part of you, remain steady, and do not be moved by the pains of the body; the body is a vessel, and the mind is the part that judges. [illegible] Whatever is contrary to nature the mind resists; but the mind itself is free, and it is in its own power to be content.

units.la: δικήματα δικαιώματα καὶ τὰ ἀκολασήματα, καὶ τὰς λύπας, ἢ τὸν φόβους κίνησις, ὅσα ἄλλο ὅτιν, ἢ χαρισαμένου τῆς φύσεως. καὶ ὅταν δέ πνι τ[?] συμξαινόντ[?]ην δυσχεραίνει τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν, καταλέπει καὶ τόπ[?] τῷ ἑαυτοῦ χώραν. πρὸς ἰσότητα γὰρ καὶ δημοσίαν[?] καταγκάσασαι, οὐχ ἧττον ἢ πρὸς δικαιοσύνην. καὶ γὰρ τοῦτα σὶ εἴδει ἔστι τῆς κοινωνίας, μᾶλλον δὲ πρὸς ἐντέραν[?] τὴν δικαιοπραγμάτων. Ὥσπερ εἷς καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς ὅν ἀεὶ τὸ βίου σκοπὸς, ὅτι εἷς καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς δι' ὅλου τοῦ βίου ἐὰν οὐ διώκητε. ἐὰν ἀρχῇ τὸ ἐρημένον, ἐὰν μὴ κ[illegible, ~4 letters] προσθῆς, ὃ τοῦτον ἐὰν δεῖ τῆς τοῦ τὸν σκοπόν. ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐχ ἡ παν-τὴν τὴν ὀπωσοῦν πολέσει δυνοῦντην ἀγαθῶν ὑπολήψις ὁμοία ἐστὶν, ἀλλ' ἡ τῆν ποίην δέ τι-νων, τουτέσι τὴν κοινῶν, οὕτω καὶ τὰς σκοπὸς, δεῖ τὸς κοινωνικὸς καὶ πολιτι-κὸν ὑποτίθεσθαι· ὁ γὰρ εἰς ὄψιν πάσας τὰς ἰ-δίας ὁρμὰς ἀπουβλιῶν, πίστας τὰς πέξεις ὁ-μοίας ἀχρῶν[?], ἡ ἐς ὄψιν ἀεὶ ὁ αὐτὸς ἔσται. Τὸν μὲν τ[?] ὀρφὸν, ἡ τ[?] κατοικίδιον ἡ τ[?] ποίαν τοῦτα ἡ διασόσιν[?]. Σωκράτης ἢ τὰ τὴν πολιλῶν δύγματα, λεμίας ἐκάλη, παιδίων δέματα. Λακεδαιμόνιοι ζῆς μὴ ξένοις οἱ τοῖς θεωρίαις ὑπὸ τῇ σκιᾷ τὰ βάλα ἐπιθεῖναι, αἱ ἔι ἢ ἔτυχαν ἐκαθέζοντο. Τῷ Ῥοδίῳ ὁ Σωκράτης πρὸ τῇ μὴ[?] τῷ μὴ ὀρχεῖσθαι πρὸς αὐτὸν, ἵνα ἔφη μὴ ζῷ καὶ κἂν ἴσως ὀλίγῳ ἀπολάρμαι[?]. Τουτέστι μὴ δ᾽ ὑπὸ πα-θῶν οὐ δυνηθῇ αὐτὸν σύγχυσιν[?] ποιῆσαι[?].
units.tr: Injustices are just deeds and licentious acts, and the pains and fears, and whatever else there is, come from the movement of nature that has given them. When the governing part is troubled by something that happens, it also leaves room for its own domain. For it is compelled toward equality and public good no less than toward justice; indeed these too belong to the kind of fellowship, and even more so to the just conduct of affairs. Just as the goal of life is always one and the same, so the life of the whole is one and the same, if you do not pursue it. If you begin with the one thing and do not add the other, you ought to hold to the goal. For just as the opinion of good things is not the same for every kind of person, but only for certain ones, namely the common and civic, so the goals too must be set by the sociable and civic. For whoever looks to all his private impulses and does not look to the same goal will not always remain the same.

units.la: Ἐν τοῖς Ἐφεσίων γράμμασι, πρᾶγμα ἐκεῖνο συνεχῶς ἀναμιμνήσκεσθαι τῶν παλαιῶν τῆς ἀρετῇ χρηστῶν[?]. Οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι, ἐωρῶν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀφορᾶν, ἵνα ἀναμιμνήσκωνται μετὰ τῆς ἀεὶ κ[?] τὰ αὐτὰ ὡσαύτως δ᾽ ἑαυτὸν ὁρᾶν ἀναγνώσεως[?] τῆς τάξεως ἡ τῆς καθαρότητος, ἡ τῆς γυμνότητος. Οὐδὲν γὰρ πεπαιδευμένον ἄσχημον[?]. Οἷος ὁ Σωκράτης τὸ κώδιον ὑπεζωσμένος, ὅτε ἡ Ξανθίππη λαβοῦσα δὲ ἱμάτιον ἔξω πεπηλε[?]. Καὶ ἃ εἶπον ὁ Σωκράτης τοῖς ἑταίροις ἀϊσθάνεσθαι καὶ ἀναχωρήσασιν, ὅτι αὐτὸν εἶδον ὥστε ἐσαλμίον[?].
units.tr: In the Ephesians' writings, it is worth constantly recalling the men of old who were good in virtue. The Pythagoreans, seeing people look up to heaven, used to keep looking at the sky so that they might remember the things that are always the same, and so that they might see themselves in the same order, purity, and nakedness. For nothing learned is shameful. Such was Socrates, girded with his sheepskin, when Xanthippe took his cloak and threw him out. And what Socrates said to his companions when they withdrew, that they had seen him as he was, is also to be felt.

units.la: Ἐν τῷ γεγράφθαι καὶ ἀναγινώσκειν οὐ πότε-ρον ἀρξεῖς, πλὴν ἀφχῆς. ἐσῖσο τολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν τῷ βίῳ.
units.tr: In writing and reading, there is no going further than the beginning. Likewise in life, much more so. [Greek: ἐν τῷ γεγράφθαι καὶ ἀναγινώσκειν οὐ πότερον ἀρξεῖς, πλὴν ἀρχῆς]

units.la: Δῶλος τὸ φύνας[?], ὃ μέτεσί σοι λόγου.
units.tr: Deceit to what is phunas, which has a share of reason for you.
"And my dear heart laughed within me." [Greek: ἐμὸν δ᾽ ἐγέλασε φίλον ἦτορ]

units.la: Μέμνονται δ᾽ ἀρετῇ χαλεποῖς βαλλόντων ἐστασιν. Σύκην χειμῶν ζητεῖν, μαινομένου. Ζιοῦντος ὁ τὸ παιδίον ζητῆν, ὅτε ὃν ἐπὶ δίδοται. Καταφιλοῦντα τὸ παιδίον ἔλεγεν ὁ Ἐπίκτητος, Οὐδὲν ἀφιέγγεσθαι, αὔριον ἴσως ἀφανής. δύσφημα ταῦτα; οὐδὲν δύσφημον ἔφη φυσιφυσικὸν τινὸς ὁρισμὸν σημαντικόν. ἢ καὶ τὸ τοῦ σάχνας ἀκειαθῆναι, δύσφημον. ὅμφαξ, σαφυλὴ[?], σαφὶς, τὰ αὐτὰ μεταβολαί, ἐπὶ ἐς τὸ μὴ ὄν, ἢ ἐς τὸ νῦν μὴ ὄν. Λύσις πρὸς αἱρέσεως γίνεται, διὰ τῆς Ἐπικτήτου. Τέχνῳ δὲ ἔφη ποῦ δὲ συγκαταθέσεως εὑρεῖν. καὶ ἐν τῷ πρὸς τὰς ὁρμὰς τόπῳ δὲ ποιητικὴν φυλάσσειν, ἵνα μὴ ὑπεξαιρέσεως, ἵνα κοινωνικῷ, ἵνα κατ' ἀξίαν. ἡ ὀρέξεως μὲν τῶν αὐτῶν πάσιν ἀπέχεσθαι, ἐγκλίσει δὲ ἐπὶ πρὸς μηδὲν τὴν ἐκ' ἡμῖν χρῆσθαι, ὃ τοῦ τυχόντος ἐν ἔφη ὅσην ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ μένεσθαι, ἐὰν μὴ ὁ Σωκράτης ἔλεγε. τί δέ λέγετε λογικὸν ψυχὰς ἔχειν, ἢ ἀλόγων; λογικῶν. τίνων λογικῶν; ὑγιῶν, ἢ φαύλων; ὑγιῶς; τί ἂν ζητεῖτε; ὅτι ἐμῷ. τί ἂν μάχεσθε, καὶ διαφέρεσθε;
units.tr: Men are contending with bad things by virtue. A bad winter to seek, a madman's. Of one living, the child seeks, when it is given. Epictetus, kissing a child, said: "Do not utter anything inauspicious; perhaps tomorrow he will be absent." Are these ill-omened words? He said nothing ill-omened, but a sign of some natural definition. Or the rule about being healed from a scratch is also ill-omened. The same changes apply to what is not, or what is not now. Resolution comes about through choice, as Epictetus says. In the art of assent one must also find a place for impulses, to guard against what is not in our power, to be sociable, to be worthy. One should abstain from the same things as everyone and use what is in our power for nothing; not to be moved by chance, as Socrates said, to remain. What do you say, that souls have reason, or are they unreasoning? Reasoning. Which reasoning? Sound, or base? Sound. Why then do you seek? Because I am mine. Why then do you fight and quarrel?

units.la: ΜΑΡΚΟΥ ΑΝΤΩΝΙΝΟΥ αὐτοκράτορος, τῶν εἰς ἑαυτὸν βιβλίον ιβ'.
units.tr: Marcus Antoninus, Emperor, Book 12 of His Meditations to Himself.

units.la: ΠΑΝΤΑ ἐκεῖνα ἐφ' ἃ ἀλλὰ πε-ριόδου θύχη ἐλθεῖν, ἤδη ἔχειν δυνάμεως, ἐὰν μὴ σαυτῷ φιλο-σοφίας. ἔστω δ' ἕν, ἐὰν πᾶν τὸ πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ἀπαλλαγῇ, ἡ δ' μέλλον ἐπιτρέψης τῇ προνοίᾳ. ἡ δ' παρὸν μόνον ἀπόθεσις πρὸς ὀσιότητα καὶ δικαιοσύνη. ὀσιότητα μὲν, ἵνα φίλης δ' ἀρχόμενον. σοὶ γὰρ αὐτὸ ἡ φύσις ἔφερε, καὶ σὲ τούτῳ δικαιοσύνη ᾗ, ἵνα ἐλευθέρως καὶ χωρὶς περιστάσεως λέγης τὰ ταλαιπωρία, καὶ πλέον τὰ ἐν νόμῳ, καὶ κατ' ἀξίαν. μὴ ἐμπλεκόμενοι δέ σε, μήτε κακία ἀλλοτρία, μήτε ὑποτύπωσις, μήτε φωνή, μηδὲ μὲν αὐτὸς ἀνάπλησις τῷ συνεπιθαρραλέου σοι σαρκινίου. ὅ-ρα γὰρ δ' πάχος. ἐὰν δὲ ὅτι δὴ τὸ αὐτὸ πρὸς ἐξόδωνη, ὡς τὰ ἄλλα καταλιπὼν, μόνον τὸ ἡγεμονικόν σου, ἡ δ' οὐ σοί θεῖον πιμοῦς, ἡ δ' μὴ τάχυσθαί ποτε ζῶ φοβοῦ, ἀλλὰ τό γε μηδέποτε ἀρξασθαι ἐν φύσει ζῶ· ἔσῃ ἄνθρωπος ἄξιος τὸ γεννηθὲν κόσμου, καὶ τάχυσθ' ἀξιος ὢν τῆς πατρίδος, καὶ ἑκμαλίζων ὡς ἀπεσθόἀπροσδόκητα τὰ καὶ ἡμέραν γινόμενα, ὧν κρα-μαλμῷ ἐν τῇδε καὶ τῇδε. ὁ Ζεὺς πάντα τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ, γυμνὰ τὴν ὑλικὴν ἀγγείων καὶ φλοιῶν ἢ καὶ σαρκῶν [?] ὀρᾷ, μόνῳ δὲ τῷ ἑαυτοῦ νοερῷ μόνων ἅπτεται, τὸ δὲ ἑαυτὸν εἰς τοῦτο ἐρρύη-κότων ἢ ἀπαχθυμένων. ἐὰν δὲ αὐτῷ ἐθί-σῃς ποιεῖν, τὸ πολὺ ταῦτα ἐθισμὸν σεαυτὸν διαίρεσις. ὁ δὲ μὴ τὰ πολυκαμύλα ἡρεάδια ὁρῶν, ἢ πτήσῃ ἔαυτὰ, καὶ οἰκίαν, καὶ δόξαν, καὶ τῶν τοιούτων πολυολιὼ ἢ σκηνῶν ἀφώμενος, ἀχο-λήσεται, τρία ἐστὶν ἐξ ὧν σωιέσηκας, σωμάτιον ψυχάτιον, νῦς. τοῦτον τὰ Μὰ μέχρι τῷ ἀπιμε-λεῖ δὲ ἐν σὺ ὅ. ὁ δὲ τέλειον μόνον νυείως ὢν, ὃ ἐὰν χωρίσῃς ἀφ' σεαυτῷ, τοῦτ' ἐστὶν ἀφ' τῆς διανοίας, ὅσα ἄλλα ὁρίσῃ ἢ λέγῃ ἢ ὅσα αὐτὸς ἐποίησας ἢ εἶπας, καὶ ὅτι ὡς μέλλοντα ταράχσεις, ἢ ὅσα τὸ πολυκμένα σοι σωματικά, ἢ τὸ συμ-φύτω πνευματικὸς, ἀποκαίςετα πέρσειν, ὃ ὅ-σα ἢ ἔξωθεν πολιεῖτα δίνῃ ἐλίας, ὥστε τ' ξωφμαχριλίων [illegible, ~12 letters] καὶ τὴν νοερὰν διὰ μὲν ἀπόλυσον ἐφ' ἑαυτὸ ζῷῳ, ποιοῦσαν τὰ δίκαια, ὃ ἥλεῖσαν τὰ συμβαίνοντα, καὶ λέγω-σαν τἀληθῇ, ἐὰν χωρίσης φαμὶ τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν τὸ τὰ πεποιημένα ἐν πεπαιδεύσῃ, καὶ τὸ χρόνῳ τὰ ἐσπένδνα, ἢ τὰ πεφωχῶτα, ποιήσης τε σεαυτῷ, οἷος ὁ Ἐμπεδόκλεος σφαῖρος κυκλοτόρης τῆς κοινῆς συνθείη γαίων, μένοντι ζῷω ἐμμε-λετήσης ὁ ζῆς, τοῦτέστι τὸ πῖον, διώκειν τὸγ μέ-χρι τῆ ἀποθανεῖν ἀπολειπομένου, ἀπεξάκ-τως καὶ ὑγιενῶς, καὶ ιλίως τῷ σαυτῷ σύμμονι διαβιῶναι. Πολλάκις ἐθυμάσα, πῶς ἑαυτὸν μᾶλλον ταύτῃ φιλεῖ, τὴν δὲ ἑαυτὸν πε-ρὶ αὐτῆς ὑπολήμψει ὁ ἐλάττονι λόγῳ πίστευε, ἢ τῷ τ' ἄλλων. Ἐάν γοῦν τινὰ Θεὸς ὠφ[?]ελήσας, ἢ δι-ἀδικηθεὶς ἐμφρων καλὸν μηδὲ καθ' ἑαυτὸν ἀμυμεῖας καὶ διανοείας, ὃ μὴ ἀ[?] μαγκ[?] γινώσκων ἐξοίσει, ἀλλὰ πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν ἔτω[?] τοῖς τέλας μᾶλλον αὐδ[?]ρίμεθα τί ποτε τοι-εὶ ἡμῶν φρονήσουσιν, ἢ ἑαυτούς. Πῶς ποτε πάντα καλῶς καὶ φιλανθρώπως διατάξαντες οἱ Θεοί, ὅσον μόνον παρέδον, διότι[?] οὕτως τὴν ἀνθρώ-πων καὶ πάντων χρηστούς, καὶ πολλὰ ἔτι πρὸς Θεὸν ὥσπερ συμβόλαια ἡμῖν, καὶ ὑπὸ πολλῶν δι' ὀρῶν ὁσίων καὶ ἱεροφυλάκων ζωὴν θείῳ γενομένης, ἐπειδὰν ἅπαξ ἀρχθῶσι, μηκέτι ἀλλὰ γίνεσθαι, ἀλλ' ἐς τὸ παντελές ἀπο-ξηρᾶναι. Ὅσον δὲ ἐπὶ ἡμῖν καὶ ὅταν ἔχει, οὐ λαθὼν ὅτι εἰ ὡς ἑτέρως ἔχειν ἔδει, ἐποίησεν ἄν. Ἐὰν γὰρ δίκαιον ᾖ, ᾧ ἄν καὶ δίωκτον. Καὶ ἡ κατὰ φύσιν, ἀνάγκη ἂν αὐτὸ ἡ φύσις. Ἐπὶ δὲ τῶ μὴ ὅταν ἔχειν, ἐπὶ δὲ χρὴ ὅταν ἔχει, πείθω σοι τὸ μὴ δι-ὠσθαι ὅτω γίνεσθαι, ὁρᾷς ἢ καὶ αὐτὸς, ὅτι ὅσον πραξηπραξιν τὴν δικαιολογίᾳ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν[?], ἐὰν δ᾽ ὅτω διελεγόμεθα τοῖς Θεοῖς, εἰ μὴ ἀρίστοι καὶ δικαιότατοί εἰσιν. ἡ δ᾽ ἕξις, ἐὰν τι πολιτ[?] δον ἀδίκως καὶ ἀλόγως ἡμεληκμένον τὴν σὺ τῇ διακοσμήσει[?]. Ἐπιζητεῖ καὶ ὅσα ἀγνοῶσκεις. καὶ γὰρ ἡ χεὶρ ἡ ἀεισερὰ πρὸς τὰ ἄλλα δι᾽ αὐτὸν ἀρχὴς ὅσα, τῇ χαλινῷ ἐρρωμένεστερον ἢ δεξιὰ κρατεῖ. ἔσχε γὰρ ἐὰν ἔτι[?]. Ὁπλον δὲ καταληφθῆναι ἐπὶ τῷ θανάτῳ, καὶ σώματι καὶ ψυχῇ τὴν βραχύτητα τοῦ βίου, πῶς ἀχαίνουσαν τῷ ὀπίσω καὶ πέρσω αἰδνος, πῶς αἰσθέντων πάσης ὕλης, γυμνὰ τὰ φλοίων [?] τὰ αἰπώδη. τὰς ἀναφορὰς τῶν πέξεων. τί πόνος, τί ἡδονή. τί θάνατος, τί δόξα. τίς δ᾽ ἑαυτῷ ἀσχολίας αἴτιος; πῶς ἂν δεῖς ὑπ᾽ ἄλλων ἱμασθ[?]ζεται, ὅπῃ πάντα ὑπόληψις.
units.tr: All those things you hope to reach by some roundabout path you can have now, if you do not begrudge them to yourself. That is, if you let go of everything that lies in the past, entrust the future to providence, and direct the present only towards holiness and justice. Holiness, so that you accept what happens as your own nature has assigned it to you; justice, so that you speak the truth freely and without evasion, and act according to law and to each thing's worth. Let no one's wickedness, no one's opinion, no one's speech, and no sensation of your flesh, which shares the suffering, hinder you. Let the suffering stay with the part of you that suffers. If, when death comes, you let go of everything else and keep only your governing mind, and do not cling to it, but are willing to leave it as a thing that is not yours; if you are free from passion, and though you are still alive, you are not afraid of dying, but remain content whether the time is long or short, then you will be a man worthy of the world that begot you, and worthy of the fatherland that rules you. Expect the unforeseen things that happen each day, and do not be astonished at them. Zeus sees all governing minds stripped bare of their vessels and husks and flesh; he touches only the rational part, which is his own and which has come forth from him. If you train yourself to do likewise, you will be free from many troubles. He who does not look at the crowd of fine things that carry him to his house, his fame or his wealth, and does not attach himself to such things, will not be distressed. There are three things of which you are made: body, breath, and mind. Of these, the first two are yours only so far as you must care for them. Whatever else is not yours, that is, what your thought separates from you, whatever other people do or say, whatever you yourself have done or said, and whatever the future may bring that troubles you, and whatever belongs to your body and breath, and whatever the outer world sends flowing over you, so that the swirl of things washes around you, leave all these alone. Let your rational mind stay free, doing what is just, accepting what happens, and speaking the truth. Separate your governing mind from the things that come to it, and from the past and the future, and make yourself like the sphere of Empedocles, rounded and at rest, and strive to live only the life that is present to you. Be content, to the end of your life, to live with your own mind without hindrance or disturbance, and at peace. Often I have wondered how each man loves himself more than others, yet puts less trust in his own judgement of himself than in the opinions of others. If a god or a wise teacher should appear to someone and bid him not to think or plan anything within himself without speaking it aloud, he could not bear it even for a single day; we are more concerned what people will think of us than what we think of ourselves. How is it that the gods, who have arranged all things well and kindly, have left only this one thing unordered: that some of the best men, who have made covenants with the gods and who through many holy deeds have consecrated their lives to the divine, once they have died, do not live again, but are utterly extinguished? But as for what remains with us, whenever it occurs, we must not forget that, if things had to be otherwise, the gods would have made them otherwise. For what is just is also possible, and what is according to nature, nature itself would necessarily bring about. From this reasoning about what is and what is not to be, and what must be, I persuade you that you should not be disturbed by what happens. You see, too, that the discussion with the gods about what is just is the same as with the gods themselves, if they are not the best and most just. The habit, if anything is neglected unjustly and without reason, is to be left to the ordering of the whole. Seek also what you do not know. For the hand, when it is used for other purposes, is held by its own nature, and the bridle holds the horse more firmly than the right hand does. Be prepared to be seized by death, and in body and soul to endure the brevity of life, so that you may look back and forward at everything as a whole, and see the things of the flesh stripped of their husks, and the passions of the flesh and their driving forces. What is pain? What is pleasure? What is death? What is fame? Who is the cause of your troubles? How can a man be disturbed by others, when everything depends on opinion?

units.la: Ὁμοίως δ᾽ ἐν δεῖ ἐν τῇ τῆς δογματικῆς χρήσει, παγκράτιασι, οὐχὶ μονομαχῶ. ὁ μὲν γὰρ τὸ ξίφος ὧν χρῆται, ἀφαιρεῖται καὶ ἀναιρεῖται, ὁ δὲ τῇ χεῖρα ἀεὶ ἔχει, ἡ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ συσχεῖν αὐτῇ δεῖ. Θεωροῦντα τὰ πράγματα ὁρᾶν διαιρούντα εἰς ὕλην, αἴτιον, ἀναφοράν. ἠλίκῳ ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ἄνθρωπος μὴ ποιεῖν ἄλλο, ἢ ὅπερ μέλλει ὁ Θεὸς ἐπαινεῖν. καὶ δέχεσθαι πάντα, ὃ ἂν νέμῃ αὐτῷ ὁ Θεός. τὸ ἐξῆς τῇ φύσει, μήτε Θεοῖς μεμπτέον. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἑκόντες ἢ ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι, μήτε ἀνθρώπῳ, ἰδὲν. ὃδα γὰρ ἐχὶ ἀκούντας, ὥστε ὃδαί μεμπῆσθαι[?]. πῶς γέλοιος καὶ ξένος ὁ θαυμάζων ὅπως τὴν ἐν τῷ βίῳ γινομένων[?].
units.tr: Likewise, in the use of principles, you must act like a pancratiast and not like a swordsman. The swordsman puts down his weapon and is killed; the pancratiast always keeps his hand free and needs only to grip. Consider things, and see them divided into matter, cause, and relation. How much freedom a man has not to do anything except what God is going to approve, and to accept everything God assigns to him. We must not blame the gods, for they do not sin willingly or unwillingly, nor blame men, for they sin only unwittingly. How ridiculous and strange is the man who is amazed at what happens in life.

units.la: Ἡ ἀνάγκη ἁμαρμένη[?], ἀπράκτος τάξις, ἢ πρόνοια ἱλάσιμος ἢ φύρμος ἐκ καινότητος ἀποσάτης. εἰ μὲν ἀπράκτος ἀνάγκη, τί ἀντιτείνεις[?]; εἰ δὲ πρόνοια, ἐχόμενη τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι, ἄξιον αὐτὸν τοιοῦτον εἶναι τῆς θεοῦ βοηθείας. εἰ δὲ φύρμος ἀνηγμόνυτος, ἀσπάζου, ὅτι σὺ τοιούτῳ ζῷ κλύδωνι· αὐτὸς ἔχεις σὺν σαυτῷ τινὰ νοῦν ἡγεμονικόν[?]. κἂν συμφέρῃ σε ὁ κλύδων, ἀπαφερέτω σαρκίδιον τὸ πνευμάτιον, τἄλλα· ἴν γὰρ νοῦν οὐ ποιεῖ. ἡ μὲν τῆς λύχνου φῶς μέχρι σβέσεως, φαίνει, καὶ τὴν αὐγὴν ἐν ἀχρειάλλει[?]· ἡ δὲ ἐν σοὶ ἀλήθεια καὶ δικαιοσύνη καὶ σωφροσύνη, προσαποσβήσεται[?]; ἀλλὰ τὰ φαντασίαν προσχόντες ὅτι ἡμάρτες[?]· τί δὲ αἱ οἶδα εἰ ἔκρινα ἁμάρτημα[?]. εἰ δὲ καὶ ἡμάρτον, ὅτι κατέκλεινεν αὐτὸς ἑαυτόν. καὶ ὅταν ὅμοιον ἔχω, ζῷ καταφρονήσῃς τὸ ἑαυτῷ ὅμως[?]. ὅτι ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸν φαῦλον ἁμαρτάνειν, ὁμοίως τῷ μὴ θέλοντι τὴν συκῆν ὁ τῶν οὐ τοῖς σύκοις φέρειν, τὰ βρέφη κλαυθμυρίζεσθαι, καὶ τὸν ἵππον χρεμετίζειν, καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα ἀναγκαῖα. τί γὰρ πάθῃ τῷ ἔξιν ἔχειν τοιαύτῃ. εἰ δὲν γοργὸς εἶ, ταύτῃ ἀπαράπτυεσθαι[?]. εἰ μὴ καθήκει μὴ πέξης[?]. ἐμὴ ἀληθὴς δόξα[?], μὴ εἴπῃς. ἡ γὰρ ὁρμή σου ἔσω, εἰς τὸ πᾶν ἀεὶ ὁρᾶν, τί ἐστιν αὐτὸ ἐκεῖνο τὸ τὴν φαντασίαν σοι ποιοῦν, ἡ ἀναπνύας[?] διαιροῦντα, εἰς τὸ αἴτιον, εἰς τὸ ὑλικὸν, εἰς τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἰς τὸν χρόνον, οὕτως ἂν πεπαῦσθαι αὐτὸ δεῖσει[?]. Αἴσθου ποτέ, ὅτι κρεῖττόν ἐστι καὶ δαιμονιώτερον ἔχεις ἐν σαυτῷ, τὰ τὰ πάθη ποιούντων, ἢ καθάπαξ τὴν νδυρωπαπούντην σε· τί μὲς νῦν ἐστιν ἢ δαίνοια. μὴ φόβος; μὴ ἐπιθυμία; μὴ ἄλλό τι τοιοῦτον; Πρῶτον, τὸ μὴ ἐκὴν, μηδὲ ἄνθρ ἀναφορᾶς. δεύτερον, τὸ μὴ ἐπ' ἄλλό τι, ἢ ὡς τὸ κοινωνικὸν τέλος τῇ ἀναγρῳ ποιεῖσθαι, ὅτι μετ' οὐ πολὺ, οὐδεὶς οὐδαμοῦ ἔσῃ, οὐδὲ τόπον τι ἃ νῦν βλέπεις, οὐδὲ τοῦτον τίς τὴν νῦν βιοῦντα. πάντα γὰρ μεταβάλλει καὶ τρέπεσθαι καὶ φθείρεσθαι τέφυκεν, ἵνα ἕτερα ἐφεξῆς γίνηται. ὅτι πάντα ἡ ὑπόληψις· καὶ αὐτὴ ἐπὶ σοι. ἄρον δὴ ὅτε ἡλιαῖς τὴν ὑπόληψιν, καὶ ὥσπερ κάμψαντι τὴν ἄκρον γαλήνην, σα[illegible, ~3 letters] ἡ πάντα, καὶ κόλπῳ ἀνύμφον. μία καὶ ἥτις ὃν ἐνέργεια ἐν καιρῷ ταυσωμένη, οὐδὲν κακὸν πάσχει, καλὸ πέπαυται, ὃ ὃ πλάξας τὴν πλᾶξιν παῦτῳ, κατ' αὐτὸ τοῦτο, καὶ ὃ πέπαυται, κακόν τι πέπονθεν. ὁμοίως δὲ ὁ ἐκ πασῶν τῶν πλήξεων σύνημα ὅπερ ἐστιν ὁ βίος, ἐὰν ἐν καιρῷ παύσηται, οὐδὲν κακὸν πάἡ κατ' αὐτὸ τοῦτο, καὶ ἀφ' ὃ ἑκάστου πάντως, ἡ κατὰ πάντας ὁ καιρῷ τὸ ἐρμὸν ἔχον, καὶ κατὰ ἰδιαίτερον δὲ ἡ κατὰ ἕκαστον[?] μέρη, ὡς ἔστιν, καὶ ὁ ὅρος δὲ φύσεως, τοῦτο μὲν καὶ ἡ ἰδία, ὅταν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ, τοιαύτη δὲ ἡ τῆς ὅλης. Ἢ τὴν μερίδα μετὰ ἄλλον, νεκρὸς ἀεὶ ὁ ἀκμαῖος ὁ σύμπας κόσμος διαμένει. Καλὸν δὲ ἀεὶ τοῦτο καὶ ὡραῖον τὸ συμφέρον τῷ ὅλῳ. Ἡ ἐν καταπαύσει τοῦ βίου, ἐκεῖσε οὐ κακὸν μὲν, ὅτι ἐδὲ αἰσχρόν. Ἐπὶ τὸ ἀποσπασθὲν, ἡ ἐν ἀκινήτου, ἀγαθὸν δὲ, ἐπὶ τῷ ὅλῳ καλὸν, καὶ συμφέρον, καὶ συμφερόμενον. Ὅτι γὰρ καὶ διοροφόρητος ὁ φερόμενος κατὰ ταῦτα θεῶν, ἐν τούτοις τῇ γνώμῃ φερόμενος.
units.tr: Fate, or unchangeable order, or providence that is gracious, or confused mixture arising from chance: if it is unchangeable necessity, why do you resist? If it is providence, then be worthy of the divine help that it offers. If it is a confused mixture without guidance, then be thankful that you are carried along in such a flood; you have within you a governing mind of your own. And even if the flood carries away your body and breath, the mind will not be carried away. For the light of a lamp shines until it is put out, and does its work even in darkness; shall the truth, justice, and temperance within you be extinguished before you die? If you are led astray by appearances, do not therefore reject what is true. Whatever you think you judged wrongly, you can correct; but if you judged wrongly, it is because your own choice led you into error. And when you have no proof of it, do not despise it, but hold to what is yours. For he who does not want the bad man to sin is like the man who does not want the fig tree to bear figs, or infants to cry, or the horse to neigh, or whatever else is necessary. For what can you do, having such a nature? If you are irritable, deal with it in that way; if it is not fitting, do not do it; if it is your true opinion, do not say it. Your impulse within is always to look at the whole; consider what that thing is which makes the appearance for you, and divide it into cause, matter, relation, and time, and then it will cease to trouble you. Perceive at some time that you have within you something stronger and more divine than the things that cause your passions or draw you about like a puppet. What is my mind now? Is it fear? Is it desire? Is it something else like this? First, do nothing at random, or without relation to the common good. Second, remember that soon you will be nothing, and nowhere, and that none of the things you now see will remain, nor the people who now live. For all things change, turn, and are destroyed by nature, so that others may come after them in order. Everything is opinion, and that too is in your power. Take away your opinion, and like a sailor who has rounded a headland, you will find a calm sea and a still bay. One action, when it stops at its proper time, suffers no harm, and he who has stopped it is not harmed either, for it is in that very act that it has ceased. Likewise, the whole sum of blows that is life, if it stops at the right time, suffers no evil, and he who stops it is not harmed. The time and measure of each thing is in its place, and the measure of nature is the same for the part as for the whole. Let the part be taken away as a man is, and the whole world will remain vigorous and young. What is good for the whole is always beautiful and fitting. The end of a life is not an evil, nor shameful, since it does not depend on our choice; it is good for the whole, beautiful, and useful, and in harmony with the whole. For the one who is carried along by the gods in this way is carried by the gods, and in these things he is carried by his own judgement.

units.la: Τεῖα τούτων δὲ πρόχειρα ἔχων, ἀπὸ μὲν ὧν τοιαύτης, ἐὰν μὴ τε εἴη, μηδὲ ἄλλως ἢ ὡς ἂν ἡ δίκη αὐτὴ συνεργήσει. Ἀπὸ δὲ τὴν ἔξωθεν συμβαινόντων, ὅπ ἦν κατ' ἀτυχίας, ἢ κ' πρόνοιαν. Ὅτε δὲ τῇ ἀτυχίᾳ μεμπτέον ὅτε τῇ πρόνοιᾳ ἐγκλητέον. Δῆλον, ὅ τι οἷον ἕκαστον ἀπὸ σερήματος, μέχρι φυχώσεως, καὶ ἀπὸ φυχώσεως, μέχρι τῆς τοῦ φυχικοῦ ἀφεῖναι, ἢ ἐξ οἰκίον ἢ σύγκλεισις, καὶ ἐς οἷα ἡ λύσις. Τέλειον, εἰ οὕτω μετέωρος ἐξαρθεὶς κατασκευάζοι τὰ ἀνθρώπεια, καὶ τῶν πολυτροπίαν ὅσα κατανοήσεις· ζωσιδῶν ἅμα, καὶ ὅσον τὸ πολιοικῆς, ἐλαιείων ἢ αἰκιλείων. Ἢ ὅτι σοί ποτε αὖ ἐξαρ-
units.tr: Keeping these things ready to hand: regarding what comes from such a cause, let it be only as justice itself would co-operate. As for what happens from outside, whether through misfortune or through providence, one must blame neither misfortune nor find fault with providence. It is clear that each thing, from its beginning to its end, and from the making of a living thing to its release from the body, whether by dissolution or by some other separation, ends in some outcome. It is fine if, lifted up on high in this way, you survey human affairs and see how varied they are, both the things that are done and the things that are suffered, whether in the affairs of the city, of the sea, or of the field.

units.la: ἡς,[?] ῆς, τοῦτα ὄφ[?]. τὸ ὁμοιοῦς, ἀ ὀλιγοχρόνιον. ἐπὶ τούτοις, ὁ τύφΘ. Βάλε ἔξω τὴν ὑπόλημψιν, σῶσαι. τίς ἂν ὁ κωλύων ἐκεῖνο; Ὅταν δυσφορῇς ἐπί τινι, ἐπελάθου τῷ, ὅτι πάντα κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν γίνεται· καὶ τοῦ, ὅτι ἁμαρτανόμενον ἀλλότριον. καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις τῷ, ὅτι ἂν δ' γινόμενον ὅτως ἀεὶ ἐγίνετο, καὶ γενήσεται καὶ νῦν πάντα ἀχῦ γίνεται. τῷ, ὅτι ἡ συγγένεια ἀνθρώπου πρὸς πάντα τὸ ἀνθρώπειον φιλῶ. οὐ γὰρ αἱματίου, ἢ σπερματίου, ἀλλὰ νοῦ κοινωνία. ἐπελάθου δὲ καὶ τῷ, ὅτι ὁ ἕκαστου νοῦς θεὸς, καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἐρρύηκε. τῷ, ὅτι ἡ δόξα ἴδιον δόξης· ἀλλὰ καὶ δι' τινιον, καὶ δι' σωματίον, καὶ αὖ δι' ψυχάριον ἐκεῖθεν ἐλήλυθον. τῷ, ὅτι πάντ' ὑπόλημψις. τῷ, ὅτι τὸ πρὸν μόνον ἕκαστος ζῇ, καὶ τὸ ὅσον ἀφ-ελάμει. σωιεχῶς ἀναπολᾶν, οὐ ἐπί τινι λίαν ἀγανακτήσαντας, οὐ οἱ μεγίσαις δόξαις, ἢ συμφοραῖς, ἢ ἔχθρας, ἢ ὁποιοσδὴν τύχαις ἀνημά-ζαντας. εἶτα ἐφισάνφ, πῶς νῦν πάντα ἐκεῖνα; καπνὸς, ἢ ςωδὸς, ἢ μῦθ, ἢ ὃ ὃ μῦλος. συμ-πλοσπηγέτω δὲ καὶ τὸ τοιοῦτο πᾶσι, οἷον, Φά-ΕιΘ Κατυλλῖνθ ἐπ' ἀγρῷ. Λάσιος Λάπος, καὶ ΣτρπίνιΘ οἱ Βαῖαις, καὶ ΤιβέριΘ οἱ Καπρείαις, καὶ ὉνάλιΘ ΡΞφΘ, καὶ ὅλως ἂ πρὸς ὁπούν μετ' αἰσίστως Διαφορά, καὶ ὡς ὑπε εὐτελὴς τῶν τὸ κατατεινόμενον.
units.tr: Or consider that you will soon be such as this, and then perhaps be no more. Put aside your opinion, and you are saved. Who could prevent you from doing so? When you are vexed at something, remember that all things happen according to the nature of the whole; and that the wrong is another's. Remember also that whatever happens now has always happened in this way and will happen in the same way throughout all time. Remember that the kinship of man with the whole human race is one of love; for it rests not on blood or seed but on the fellowship of mind. Remember too that each person's mind is god and has flowed forth from there. Remember that nothing is one's own; even one's body, one's breath and one's little soul have come from there. Remember that everything is opinion. Remember that each of us lives only in the present moment, and that only this present moment we lose. Recall continually those who, vexed beyond measure at something, or made famous by the greatest reputations, or by misfortunes, or by enmities, or by whatever fortunes, have been raised up, and then ask yourself: where are all those things now? Smoke, ash, a story, or not even that. Let the same reflection also embrace all such things, as for example Fabius Catullinus in the country, Lusius Lupus at his estate, and Stertinius at Baiae, and Tiberius at Capri, and Velius Rufus, and altogether whatever has been pursued with a strained zeal; and how each of these things is worth little.

units.la: ¶ Ὅσῳ φιλοσοφώτερον δ᾽ ὡδὶ τῆς δοθείσης ὕλης ἑαυτὸν δίκαιον, σώφρονα, θεοῖς ἐπόμενον ἀφελῶς πρέχειν. ὁ γὰρ ὑπὸ ἀτυφίας τυφῷ τυφόμενος πάντων χαλεπώτατος. Πρὸς τὸν ἐπιζητοῦντας, τῷ γὰρ ἰδιῶν τῶν θεὸς, ἢ πόθεν καταληφὼς ὅτι εἰσὶν ὕτω σέξς· πρῶτον μὲν καὶ ὀφθαλμοῖς ἐρατοί [?] ἐστιν· ἔπειτα μηδὲν ἐπὶ τῇ ἐμαυτοῦ ψυχῇ τῇ ἐμαυτοῦ ἐρασθαι [?], καὶ ὁμοίως πρῶτον. οὕτως ἂν καὶ τὸν θεοὺς, ἐξ ὧν τῆς δυναμέως αὐτῷ ἐνάσοτι πεῖραν, ἐν ταύτην ὅπῃ τί ἐστι καταλαμβάνω, ἡ αἰδοῦμαι. Σωτηρία βίου, ἕκαστον δὲ ὅλον αὐτὸ τί ἐστιν ὁρᾷν· τί μὲν αὐτῷ τὸ ὑλικὸν, τί δ᾽ αἰτιῶδες. ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ δίκαια ποιεῖν, καὶ τἀληθῆ λέγειν. τί λοιτὸς, ἢ ἀφελαῖ· ἢ ὑπὸ τῷ ζῷ σωμάτιον τὰ ἄλλο ἐπ᾽ ἄλλῳ ἀγαθὸν, ὥστε μηδὲ δ᾽ βραχύτατον διάστημα ἀφελεῖπειν. Ἐν φῶς ἡλίου καὶν διέρχηται τοίχοις, ὄρεσιν, ἄλλοις μυρίοις, μία οὐσία κοινή, καὶν διέρχηται ἰδίως τοιοῖς σώμασι μυρίοις. μία ψυχή, καὶν φύσεσι διέργνται μυρίαις, καὶ ἰδίαις ταῖς ἐναφαῖς. μία νοερὰ ψυχή, καὶν διακενεῖσθαι δοκῇ. τὰ μὲν οὖν ἄλλα μέρη τὴν ἐρημίων, οἷον τινὰ μάτα καὶ ξωοκεῖμενα, αἰσθητικὰ καὶ ἀνοικείωτα ἀλλήλοις, καί τι κἀκεῖνα δ᾽ ἓν ἰδοῦν συνέχει, καὶ τὸ ἔπειτα αὐτὰ βρῖδον διά-
units.tr: The more philosophically one does this, the more one shows oneself simply to be just, temperate and following the gods, to be open about the matter that has been given. For he who is puffed up by lack of self-knowledge is the most difficult of all men. As to those who seek: for how do you know that there are gods, or whence have you grasped that they exist in this way? First, indeed, they are lovely to the eyes; then, as I myself have never loved my own soul, so too I have not loved them first. Thus indeed by these gods, from whose power I have a clear proof, I grasp in this way what they are, or else I feel reverence. The preservation of life lies in seeing each thing as a whole: what it is in its matter and what it is in its cause. It lies in doing what is just with the whole soul and in speaking the truth. What more remains but to enjoy life and to do good, one thing after another, so that not even the smallest interval is left empty? One light of the sun passes through walls, mountains and countless other things; one common substance passes through countless bodies of the same kind; one soul passes through countless natures and individual forms; one intelligent soul passes through all, even though it seems divided. The other parts, however, that are without reason, such as inert things and things that are only fashioned, insensible and unable to be joined to one another, are held together by a single bond, and then, though they are bound together, they are pushed apart by the intellect.

units.la: νοια οὐκ δὲ ἰδίως ὡδὶ τὸ ὁμόφυλον γίνεται, καὶ συ-νίσταται, καὶ ᾗ διέρχεται τὸ κοινωνικὸν πάθος.
units.tr: Yet the kindred element is not thus formed and constituted by a separate intellect; through it the common feeling passes.

units.la: Τί ὠδὶ ζητεῖς; τὸ δλ γίνεσθαι; ἀλλ᾽ ἢ αἰσθάνεσθαι; β᾽ ὁρμᾶν; τὸ αὔξεσθαι; τὸ λέγειν αὐτῆς; τὸ φωνῇ χρῆσθαι; τὸ διανοεῖσθαι; τί τούτην [?] τὸ ὅλον σοι ἄξιον δοκεῖ; εἰ δὲ ἕκαστα ἐὐκαταφρόνη-τα, πρόσιθι ὡδὶ τελευταῖον, τὸ ἐπαινῶ λόγῳ καὶ τοῦ θεοῦ. ἀλλὰ μάχεται τοῦ τιμᾶν ταῦτα, τὸ ἀχθέσθαι. ἢ ᾧ τῷ τεθνηκέναι σεμνύεσθαι τις αὐτὴν; Ποσὸς μέρος τῆς ἀπείρου καὶ ἀχανοῦς αἰῶνος ἀφορισθέντα ἑκάσῳ. ταῦτα γὰρ ἀναφαίνεται τοῦ ἀϊδίου. τόσον δὲ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας; πόσον δὲ τῆς ὅλης ψυχῆς; οὐ τοσοῦτῳ βωλαίῳ τῆς ὅλης γῆς ἕρπεις; σαν τὰ ταῦτα οὐ δυμάμεθ᾽, μηδὲ μέγα φαντάζε, ἢ τὸ ὡς μὲν ἡ σὴ φύσις ἄγει, πρὸς ἐν. πάλιν δὲ, ὡς ἡ κοινὴ φύσις φέρει, πῶς ἔχει τοῦ χρῆται τὸ ἡγεμονικόν. οὐ γὰρ τούτῳ τὸ πᾶν ἔστι. τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ, ἃ πρόσεστί ἐστιν, ἢ ἀπρόσεστα, νεκρὰ καὶ καμπνὸς. Πρὸς θάνατον καταφρόνησιν ἐγερτικώτατον, ὅτι καὶ οἱ τῷ ἡδονῇ ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸν πόνον κακὸν κεῖνοντες, ὅμως τότε καταφρονῶσιν. Ὧ τὸ δίκαιον μόνον ἀγαθὸν, καὶ ἕως τὸ τελέους ἐπὶ λόγον ὀρθὸν πράξεις ἀφ᾽ δ᾽ ναι, τῷ ὀλιγοτόρας, οὐ ἴσως ἐστί, ἢ ὧν τὸν κόσμον θεᾶσθαι τελέουν ἢ ἑλαχίστου χρόνῳ οὐ διαφέρει, τούτῳ
units.tr: Why do you seek such things? To come into being? Or to perceive? To feel impulse? To grow? To speak? To use the voice? To think? Which of these seems to you worth so much? If you despise each of them, proceed to the last, which is to praise reason and God. But to honour these things, to be vexed by them, conflicts with this. Or is there some glory in having died? What a small part of the infinite and boundless eternity is allotted to each! For these things are seen in the eternal. And how much of the whole substance, and how much of the whole soul? And how small a clod of the whole earth do you crawl upon? Consider these things, and do not imagine great things, but rather that you are going forth from your own nature, and into the common nature, and that the reason which governs is not the whole of you. The remaining things, which are added to you or not, are dead and smoke. Nothing is more effective in stirring one up to contempt of death than the thought of those who consider pleasure the good and pain the evil, and yet despise death nonetheless. For the one who regards only the just as good, and who, as far as possible, acts according to right reason, whether for a short time or a long one, does not care whether he has contemplated the world for a shorter or a longer span, since it makes no difference to him. For him death is not terrible.

units.la: [?] Several words in this Greek are blurred and could not be read with certainty; the marked readings are best guesses. τούτῳ οὐδὲ ὁ θάνατος φοβερόν. Ἄνθρωπε, ἐπιλιτδύσω σοι τῇ μεγάλῃ ταύτῃ πόλει; τί σοι διαφέρει ἡ τῶν πέντε ἔτη; Τὸ γὰρ κατὰ τοὺς νόμους, ἴσον ἑκάστῳ. Τί οὖν δεινὸν ἡ τῆς πόλεως ἀπωτέμπει σε οὐ τύραννος, οὐδὲ δικαστὴς ἄδικος, ἀλλ' ἡ φύσις ἡ ἀποδεξαμένη; οἷον εἰ κωμῳδὸν ἀπολύοι τῆς σκηνῆς ὁ πρωταγωνιστής. ἀλλ' ἔτι εἰπὸν τὰ τῶν πέντε μέρη, ἀλλὰ τὰ τέλη. καλῶς εἶπας, ἀλλ' ὅμως τῷ βίῳ τὰ τέλη ὅλον δ' ὁρᾶμάζει. τὸ γὰρ τέλειον, ἐκεῖνος ὃ εἶζει. ὁ τότε μὲν τῆς συγκρίσεως, νῦν δὲ τῆς διαλύσεως αἴτιος, οὐ δὲ αἰνεῖ πῶς ἀμφοτέρων. ἄπῃ-ἦν ἵλεως, καὶ γὰρ ὁ ἀχ-λύων ἵλεως.
units.tr: Man, does the great city wrong you by sending you away? What difference do five years make to you? For what is according to the laws is equal for all. What then is dreadful about it, if the city sends you away, not as a tyrant or an unjust judge, but as nature who admitted you? It is as if the protagonist dismissed an actor from the stage. But, you say, I have not finished the five acts, only some of them. Well said; but in life the complete course is not the same as the final act. For the one who is the cause of your composition and of your dissolution is the same; and you are not responsible for either. Depart, then, with a gracious mind, for he who dismisses you is gracious.

units.la: ΤΕΛΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΑΝΤΩΝΙΝΟΥ ιβ' ΒΙΒΛΙΟΝ.
units.tr: The end of the twelfth book of Antoninus.
WILHELM XYLANDER OF AUGSBURG: Brief Notes.
ON THE METAMORPHOSES of Antoninus Liberalis.
1 In Cragaleus had calmed.) ποιῆσαι πλασσάνις[?]; I read παῦσαι.

units.la: 2 VI. Sacriq; custos fulminis.) τὸ ἱερὸν σιδηροῦν[?]. legi, τὸν ἱερὸν σιδηροῦν.
units.tr: 2 VI. And the guardian of the sacred thunderbolt.) τὸ ἱερὸν σιδηροῦν[?]. I read τὸν ἱερὸν σιδηροῦν.

units.la: 3 VII. Quòd ipsum destituisset.) Ad verbum ἐχῶ[?] refertur etymon. cuius varia significata apud Grammaticos est inuenire. Ego αὐτὸν legi: & λαμῶνα, pro χαμῶνα[?] reposui.
units.tr: 3 VII. Because he had abandoned him.) The etymology is referred to the verb ἐχῶ[?], whose various meanings can be found among the grammarians. I have read αὐτὸν, and restored λαμῶνα in place of χαμῶνα[?].
In this way.) I read ἅτω[?], since I found ἅπω[?].

units.la: Pellus Erodij genus est. De ephippo dubito: & fortasse est legendum ἵππῳ, equo.
units.tr: Pellus is a kind of Erodius. I am doubtful about the ephippus, and perhaps it should be read ἵππῳ, "to the horse."

units.la: 4 X. Κελεύντων[?]. ) Ego quid vocis hoc sit, non inuenio. itaq; asteriscum loco versionis posui. Caeterum multa passim perspicuè depravata, ex ingenio ac sensu correxi: quæ omnia annotare non erat operæ pretium.
units.tr: 4 X. Κελεύντων[?].) I cannot find what this word means, and so I have put an asterisk in place of a translation. Elsewhere I have corrected many passages that were plainly corrupt, by judgement and by sense; to annotate all of these would not have been worth the effort.

units.la: 5 XII. In Cygno vini vi est obrutus.) Ἐχαρακώθη[?]. lego ἐκαρώθη[?]. Post vbi asteriscum signaui, tenor fabulæ ex VII Ouidij Metamorph. potest intelligi: ad quod opus illustrandum, hic liber non parum potest adferre adiumenti. Ibi Hyrie est, quæ hæc Thyria. fortasse hoc rectius. Ego in uertendo, sensum sæpe, etiam verbis male cohærentibus in textu expressi. Cuius rei (ut unum exemplum citem) habes cuiusdam indicium in fab. XXXVIII. de Acasto & Peleo: cuius rei Horatius in Oda ad Asteriam meminit. Annotando autem omnia persequi neque volui, neque erat otium.
units.tr: 5 XII. In the Swan he was overwhelmed by the force of wine.) Ἐχαρακώθη[?]. I read ἐκαρώθη[?]. Where I have marked an asterisk, the drift of the story can be understood from Book VII of Ovid's Metamorphoses, and this book can bring not a little help to illustrating that work. There it is Hyrie, which here is Thyria; perhaps this is more correct. In translating, I have often expressed the sense even where the words in the text are poorly connected. Of this practice (to cite one example) you have an indication in fable XXXVIII, on Acastus and Peleus, which Horace mentions in his Ode to Asterie. I have not wished to pursue everything in annotation, nor was there leisure.

units.la: Valde prodigiosæ sunt hæ siue fabulæ, siue historiæ. Dico, siue historiæ: quia nimium patrocinari videntur diabolo, multoq; meliorem minusq; timendum facere, qui nihil tale factum fuisse, aut fieri posse ipsius artibus putant. Alioqui quæ de Buplago referuntur, & horum similia, plane figmentum esse, cur quis credat, causæ sunt satis iustæ. Ego in medio rem relinquo. Primæ narrationis caput deest. Videtur summa hæc esse: Philinnam Damostrati & Charitus filiam, clàm cum hospite Machata, etiam vita functam consueuisse, idq; nutricem deprehendisse.
units.tr: These stories, whether they are fables or histories, are very marvellous. I say "or histories" because they seem to lend too much support to the devil, and make him much better and less to be feared, for those who think that nothing of the kind ever happened, or could happen, by his arts. Otherwise there are good enough grounds for holding that what is related of Buplagus, and things like it, is plainly fiction. I leave the matter open. The beginning of the first narrative is missing. The gist seems to be this: Philinna, daughter of Damostratus and Charitus, secretly lived with the guest Machatas even after she was dead, and her nurse discovered this.

units.la: 1 In Ætoliam.) In Græco omnino est, εἰς Ἰτα-λίαν[?] mendose.
units.tr: 1 Into Aetolia.) The Greek has, altogether, "into Italy" [εἰς Ἰταλίαν], which is an error.

units.la: 2 Thrinaciamq;.) Θρινακίαν[?]: Siciliam nimirum. Nam tametsi peruulgatum est, eam infulam à tribus nobilibus promontorijs dictam esse τρινα-κρίαν[?] ηρίαν[?]: tamen & apud Suidam θρίναξ[?] Sicilia: vt puto, dicta à ventilabro, cuius in tanta fertilitate ea in insula plurimus vsus fuit. ne quid de falce dicam.
units.tr: 2 Thrinacia.) [Θρινακίαν]: that is, Sicily, of course. For although it is very commonly held that the island was named from its three noble headlands [τρινακρίαν], yet Suidas also has [θρίναξ] for Sicily. I think it was named from the winnowing fan, since in such great fertility the island made the most use of it, not to mention the sickle.

units.la: 3 Romam perlatis.) Ἀναλωθέντων[?]. Mallem ἀναλωθέντων[?], multo magis ἀναλωθέντων[?].
units.tr: 3 Carried to Rome.) [Ἀναλωθέντων]. I would prefer [ἀναλωθέντων], and much more [ἀναλωθέντων].

units.la: 4 Nisæ quando.) Annotatum est de his aliquid in Pyrrhum Plutarchi, à nobis. Codex hic Νυσαῖαν[?] per u habet constanter. Apud Strabonem lib. XI. Plin. lib. 6. cap. 25. Et in Dionysio Afro, ibiq; Eustathio, & eodem in Iliad. ß. 558 denique apud Suidam, vbi series litterarum ambiguitati obstat, perlegitur. quod & secutus sum. Caeterum ad hunc locum in margine annotata sunt, quæ sequuntur, & in quibus legendis ob rarissimam & obscurissimam characterum ab vsitatioribus discrepantiam me nonnihil torsi. μεταξὺ Σουσιανῆς καὶ Βακτριανῆς τόπος ἐστὶ Καταστίγωνα[?], ὅπερ ἑλληνιστὶ νῆσον[?] σημαίνει[?]. ἐνταῦθα ἵπποι διάφοροι γίνονται[?], εἰσὶ δὲ πᾶσαι ξανθαί[?]. Ὁ δὲ Εὐριπίδης[?] τὴν ἐρυθρὰν θάλασσαν[?] ἢ τῶν Νυσαίων φύσιν εἶναι[?]. Inter Susianam (inquit) & Bactrianam locus est Catastigona, quæ vox Græcè nesion, id est insulam, significat. Ibi equæ præstantes nascuntur, fuluæ omnes. Euripides Nesæam ad rubrum mare collocat.
units.tr: 4 Nysa, when.) Something about these matters has been noted by me in Plutarch's Pyrrhus. This manuscript consistently has [Νυσαῖαν] with a u. It is read in Strabo, book 11; Pliny, book 6, chapter 25; in Dionysius Afer, with Eustathius on him; in the same author on the Iliad, at 2.558; and finally in Suidas, where the sequence of letters is ambiguous, which I also followed. Moreover, the following notes are written in the margin at this passage, and in reading them I was somewhat troubled by the very rare and obscure forms of the letters, which differ from the more usual ones: [μεταξὺ Σουσιανῆς καὶ Βακτριανῆς τόπος ἐστὶ Καταστίγωνα, ὅπερ ἑλληνιστὶ νῆσον σημαίνει. ἐνταῦθα ἵπποι διάφοροι γίνονται, εἰσὶ δὲ πᾶσαι ξανθαί. Ὁ δὲ Εὐριπίδης τὴν ἐρυθρὰν θάλασσαν ἢ τῶν Νυσαίων φύσιν εἶναι]. "Between Susiana and Bactriana," it says, "there is a place Catastigona, which word in Greek means 'island' (nesion). There excellent horses are bred, all of them tawny. Euripides places Nysaea on the Red Sea."

units.la: 5 Meuaniæ,) Μευανία[?]. Vmbriæ vrbem esse Meuaniam, vel ex nono Liuij libro est manifestum. Notum porrò, & pro v consonante vsurpari à Græcis, cùm Latina vocabula transcribunt, hac litera destitutis. itaq; mirum non est α ex μυσανία[?] esse extritum. Horum exemplorum non dissimilia Plinius 7. 4. citat ex Annalibus, ne quis nimis Græcas esse putet has narrationes. De Consulum nominibus remitto te ad Annales.
units.tr: 5 Meuania.) [Μευανία]. That Meuania is a city of Umbria is clear even from the ninth book of Livy. It is also well known that the Greeks, when they transcribe Latin words, use [ου] or [β] for the consonant v, since they lack this letter; so it is no wonder that the alpha has been worn away from [μυσανία]. Pliny, book 7, chapter 4, cites similar examples from the Annals, lest anyone think these narratives too Greek. As for the names of the consuls, I refer you to the Annals.

units.la: 6 Oraculù satis.) λοξὸν . ἐμοὶ autem hic legi pro ἐμ̃, cùm ῥώμῃ nominatiuo casu legatur. Ϝαμφύλων appellatiuum duxi. Cætera in margine annotaui. & res digna nō est in qua laboretur. Ego ita verti, vt qui in nugis difficilibus nugari liberè statuissem: ne de hoc oraculo Delphos pro natatore mittere cogerer.
units.tr: 6 Oracle enough.) [λοξὸν]. But I have here read [ἐμοί] for [ἐμ̃], since [ῥώμῃ] is read in the nominative case. I have taken [Ϝαμφύλων] as an appellative. I have noted the rest in the margin, and it is not a matter worth labouring over. I have translated in such a way as one who had resolved to trifle freely over difficult trifles, lest I should be forced to send to Delphi for a diver about this oracle.

units.la: 7 Finibus Imperatoris.) ὀρίοις[?]. Forte ὀρτοῖς[?] hortis. Sed & suprà Euryopa Nili filia bis ponitur mendosè.
units.tr: 7 Borders of the Emperor.) [ὀρίοις]. Perhaps [ὀρτοῖς], "gardens" (hortis). But above, too, Euryope, daughter of the Nile, is wrongly put twice.
ON A FRAGMENT concerning the Olympic Games.

units.la: Λάοι ἀναντ@. ) Codex erat literis rarę formæ & antiquitatis conscriptus. aliam tamē lectionem exculpere non potui. Forte ϝασιάναντ@ scribendum fuerat. Loco ἐροτιμ, est ἐρχτ[?]λω in margine: quod adhibita διωίνῃ versus tolerat. Quid autem sit ἀμιονναῦν[?] Ego legerem ἀμμου εἰς ἄκαν. Sic Pelops Græcæ ciuitatis autor intelligeretur.
units.tr: [Λάοι ἀναντ@].) The manuscript was written in letters of a rare form and great antiquity, and I could not make out any other reading. Perhaps [ϝασιάναντ@] should have been written. In the margin, in place of [ἐροτιμ], there is [ἐρχτ[?]λω], which the verse tolerates with the aid of [διωίνῃ]. What [ἀμιονναῦν] is, I would read as [ἀμμου εἰς ἄκαν]. In that way Pelops would be understood as the founder of a Greek city.

units.la: 1 In Scyro infula.) Credo non Σκύρῳ, sed Σύρῳ legendum. Fuit enim Syrus insula patria Phoenicydi, unde Syrius dictus est. Quod qui non obseruarunt, Syriam ei patriam falso tribuerunt, ut alibi ofcenfum est.
units.tr: 1 In the island of Scyros.) I believe it should be read not Σκύρῳ but Σύρῳ. For Syros was an island, the homeland of Phoenicides, whence he was called Syrius. Those who did not notice this have falsely assigned Syria to him as his homeland, as has been shown elsewhere.

units.la: 2 Parybum.) In ecclogis Ctefiae ab Henrico Stephano editis, παράξηβος legitur, per u, nō p v, sol. 27.
units.tr: 2 Parybus.) In the fragments of Ctesias edited by Henricus Stephanus, the reading is παράξηβος, with a u, not p and v, p. 27.

units.la: 3 Idemq;, & Ammonem.) ἔτι δὲ πορ.in Græco. Fortasis non δὲ, sed δὴς legendum: ut bis eò profectus intelligatur; quod ad augendum facit miraculum. Quæstionem XXXIV, asterisum alleui, quòd Theophrastum euoluere huius loci causa non vacaret, & ἀκμιγνυμένη mutilum effet. Certè libro octauo historiæ Stirpium hodie legitur, quod hic ex septimo citat.
units.tr: 3 Again, and to Ammon.) In the Greek it is ἔτι δὲ πορ. Perhaps δὲ should be read as δὴς, so that he is understood to have gone there twice, which adds to the marvel. I have placed an asterisk beside question XXXIV, because I had no leisure to consult Theophrastus for this passage, and ἀκμιγνυμένη is mutilated. Certainly it is read today in the eighth book of the History of Plants, though he here cites it from the seventh.

units.la: 4 Clematis.) In Græco est πλίματις. Legi πλιματις, quæ vox etiam sarmentum significat. πλωματισόμενος intellexi epilepticos, quamquam nullo exemplo fretus. 382 historiæ verba plane sunt luxata.
units.tr: 4 Clematis.) In the Greek it is πλίματις. I read πλιματις, a word which also means a twig. I understood πλωματισόμενος to mean epileptics, though I rely on no example. The words of the history in this place (p. 382) are plainly dislocated.

units.la: 5 De plantis octauo.) Imò nono, ut hodie diuisi habentur. Interficere posui, quia ἀπονταῖναι ille habet, non ἐμφαίνειν. Hoc paragrapho scriptor etiam id quod de malis ulceribus sequitur, complexus est. Propter vocem ἰξίου annotatum est ad marginem: τοῖς παρ' ἐνίοις λεγομένοις νιφάοις, τοῖς ἐν τοῖς σπιλέσιμ, ὁμωνύμ' τοῖς ἐν τοῖς ἀεὶ ἐπέ-χει.
units.tr: 5 In the eighth book on plants.) Rather the ninth, as they are now divided. I have put "to destroy" because he has ἀπονταῖναι, not ἐμφαίνειν. In this paragraph the writer also includes what follows about malignant ulcers. On account of the word ixion a note has been added in the margin, saying that some call these by the name "nipha", a word homonymous with those in the "spilesimos" passage, and which always stands for the same thing.

units.la: φ σι. Σιμωνίδα καὶ τινὰ, ἢ καὶ χαμαιλέων παλέγεται. καὶ ἐτόρα ἐγὼ τις, ἀφ' ἧς ὁ ἴςος[?]
units.tr: Simonis and some others, or it is called chamaeleon. And now I, from which the ... [the text here is too corrupt to be recovered].

units.la: Ad id autem quod de Solis & Pinaro sequitur, visitatoribus characteribus recentior quispiam adscripsit, quibus ignorationem situs locorum & distantiae obijceret autori. Quanquam euanuerunt quaedam literae, ut integra legi non possint. Legi autem ἀπνυφλῶς[?] pro ἀπνύφας[?].
units.tr: As for what follows about the Sun and Pinarus, a more recent hand has written in the margin, in faded characters, by which it reproaches the author with ignorance of the position of places and of distances. Some letters have, however, vanished, so that the text cannot be read in full. I read ἀπνυφλῶς for ἀπνύφας.

units.la: 1 Cum caneret.) ἀδοντ& αὐτὸς μεταξύ[?]. Vide ne aliquid desit: nam sicicadam in fidis ruptis locū subijsse, & vicem eius gessisse, est apud Clementem Alexandrinum, initio. προτρεπτικὸς hanc fabulam referentem.
units.tr: 1 While he was singing.) I read "sing" ... Take care that nothing is missing here: for that a cicada took the place of a broken string on the lyre and performed its function is found in Clement of Alexandria, at the beginning of the Protrepticus, where he recounts this story.

units.la: 2 Septem femineos.) Ex hymno Homeri in Mercurium: sed nescio quos sit codices autoresq; secutus. Certe pro ἀκλυτέρων, hodie συμφώνας legitur.
units.tr: 2 Seven female voices.) From Homer's Hymn to Hermes, but I do not know which manuscripts or authors he followed. Certainly for ἀκλυτέρων, συμφώνας is read today.

units.la: 3 Si importentur.) In Graeco, ναὶ ἰδὼ τις: quod à posteriore mutuatus librarius videtur.
units.tr: 3 If they are brought in.) In the Greek it is ναὶ ἰδὼ τις, which the copyist seems to have borrowed from a later passage.

units.la: 4 Atrbi vsq;.) Haud dubie loci nomen excidit in Metamorphosib. Antonini, Lero insulæ adscribuntur. Vide ibi.
units.tr: 4 At Atrbi ...) Undoubtedly the name of a place has dropped out in the Metamorphoses of Antoninus, where Lero is assigned to the island. See there.

units.la: 5 Eliam.) ἠλίαν. Nescio an circa Elidem: sicut infrà §. 155. Cranonem vnico vscripsi, Aristotelem & alios secutus: cum nostler codex duobus vv scriptum habeat.
units.tr: 5 Elian.) ἠλίαν. I do not know whether it refers to Elis, as below at §155. I have written Cranon with a single n, following Aristotle and others, since our manuscript has it with two.

units.la: 6 ὃν πόλλα τίμνει.) Ex Hesiod. ε. ἔργων: vbi tamen τενδλα legitur. Mox ἐκλύεται. Sensus poscit pro ἐκλύεται.
units.tr: 6 "which many ..." From Hesiod's Works and Days, where however τενδλα is read. Soon after, ἐκλύεται. The sense requires this word in place of ἐκλύεται.

units.la: O’ vtinam.) Primo verfu lego οὐ μ’ ἐτί, non ὃ μὴ τι. quod ☧ à metro est, ☧ à sensu alienū. Sed ad βάλε ἀλλ’ βάλε in margine est annotatum, κατ’ ἀποκοπὴν τῆς Α ἀρχῆς sοιχεῖα. ἐφι γὰρ τὸ ἐλον ἀβάλε sημαντικὸν sυχὴς ἐπίρρημα, αὐτὶ τῆς ὀφελον, εἴθε, ᾅθε. βάλε ait, praecifo α prima litera, pro ἀβάλε optandi aduerbio positum.
units.tr: O that ...! In the first line I read οὐ μ' ἐτί, not ὃ μὴ τι, which is right by the metre but foreign to the sense. But at βάλε ἀλλ' βάλε a note in the margin says that, with the initial alpha cut off, the word is ἀβάλε, an adverb expressing wish, equivalent to ὤφελον, εἴθε, αἴθε. He says βάλε, with the first letter removed, used in place of the optative adverb ἀβάλε.

units.la: Tarandum.) Sic Aristotelēs θάωμας. ἀνὰς, non per τ, vt nostrum.
units.tr: So Aristotle has the form with ν, not with τ as in our text.
Cedripolis. A faulty word. Aristotle has Amphipolis.

units.la: Veluti humidis & mollibus.) ὡς αὐ ἰνὺγωμ̄ ὄντων. Cur hederam gestarent, apud Aristotelem causa nō est explicata. Hoc quidem non celatum, aliquid doloris ob cornuum deiectionem esse ceruis. Vide num non sit legendū pro ἐμ, ἔτι: vt fortassis recens enata, ☧ adhuc tenera cornua edera munierint. Quod ad vocem Achainam attinet in margine (quantum quidem ego legere possum) est Αχαϊνα ἱ☧ ἀαθίνα, ἰλίνιαι τινὲς ἐλάφων. Vide Apollonij Ἀργονωτ. ἀ. ☧ eius Scholiastam, paragr. 16. ☧ Eustath. Iliad. ϐ.
units.tr: "As when things are moist and soft." Why they wore ivy is not explained in Aristotle. This at least is not hidden: stags suffer some pain from the shedding of their horns. See whether it should not be read ἔτι for ἐμ, so that perhaps the newly sprouted, still tender horns were protected by ivy. As for the word Achaina in the margin (so far as I can read it), it says that some call them the "athina" of stags. See the first book of Apollonius' Argonautica and its scholiast, paragraph 16, and Eustathius on the second book of the Iliad.

units.la: Aliquantulum.) ὀλίγον in Græco est, nō ὀλίγας. Cætera ex Aristotelis Mirabilibus narrationibus, ☧ Plutarchi libello de comparatione animalium terrestrium ☧ aquatilium, pete.
units.tr: "A little." In the Greek it is ὀλίγον, not ὀλίγας. For the rest, look in Aristotle's Marvellous Stories and Plutarch's treatise on the comparison of land and water animals.

units.la: Prætereuntem enim.) Deest aliquid. Acsalonē diphthōgo scripsi, sicut ☧ Aristotelēs de Hist.animalium. Noster codex ε ψιλῷ habet.
units.tr: Something is missing. I have written Acsalone with a diphthong, as Aristotle does in the History of Animals. Our manuscript has a simple epsilon.

units.la: 13 Piscium solum. ) τὸν ἁλιφρὸ μόνον μὴ ρυχάζειν, non liquet: ut & in CXXXII ιεράκα ... ἀτο· ubi meo arbitratu sum usus.
units.tr: 13 Of fish only.) Whether τὸν ἁλιφρὸ μόνον μὴ ρυχάζειν is correct is not clear, as also in CXXXII, where I have followed my own judgment.

units.la: 14 Quibus ruptis. ) ἐφ' ὧν πνυνυμένων: legi ἐξ ὧν ρηγνυμένων. In XCIII. diu naui.
units.tr: 14 From which, when broken.) ἐφ' ὧν πνυνυμένων: I read ἐξ ὧν ρηγνυμένων. I have long laboured over this in XCIII.

units.la: 15 A cane. ) Legi ὑπὸ νωσός, pro τινός: quamquam res aliter loquitur. C V. non intelligo.
units.tr: 15 From a dog.) I read ὑπὸ νωσός for τινός, though the matter speaks otherwise. In CV I do not understand it.

units.la: 16 Crentile cognomen. ) ἐπιδυμίας legi, ubi habetur ἐπιθυμίας.
units.tr: 16 The Crentile surname.) I read ἐπιδυμίας, where ἐπιθυμίας is found.

units.la: 18 Nemo recte reprehendit. ) Ἀνὴρ οὐδένα λαβεῖν. ἀπαναστάς λαβεῖν, legi: nisi forte ἂν εἰ ἀνόμως malis, ut reprehendatur qui perpetuum duxerit, quod statis tantum fit temporibus.
units.tr: 18 No one rightly rebukes.) Ἀνὴρ οὐδένα λαβεῖν ... I read ἀπαναστὰς λαβεῖν, unless perhaps you prefer ἂν εἰ ἀνόμως, so that the one rebuked is he who has taken it as perpetual, when it happens only at set times.

units.la: 19 Crines flauos. ) Cum legeretur πρατάν ξανθίσσων, non obscure sensi vitiatum locum, & & scribendum πράθιν ξανθίσσων.
units.tr: 19 Yellow hair.) Since I read πρατάν ξανθίσσων, I clearly sensed the corrupt passage, and that it must be written πράθιν ξανθίσσων.

units.la: IN MARCI ANTO- NINI de vita sua libros, An- notationes.
units.tr: Annotations on the Twelve Books of Marcus Antoninus, On His Own Life.

units.la: Haud ingratam rem lectori, neque à meo instituto alienam facturus mihi videor, si principio de autore nonnihil exponam: nam de operis ipsius dignitate atque usu, in Præfatione, ea quæ visa fuerunt referen-
units.tr: I think I shall be doing the reader a service that is not unwelcome and not foreign to my plan if I first say something about the author. What seemed worth reporting about the dignity and usefulness of the work itself I have set down in the Preface.

units.la: [the note-lines above are transcribed in the main text] ferenda, posuimus. Scriptum est à M. Aurelio Antonino Vero Imperatore Romano, eo qui Philosophi cognomentum tulit. Cuius quoniam extat vita, perscripta à Dione nostro, epitomæq; Xiphilinianæ inserta, itemq; à Iulio Capitolino, & aliis: ea modo adducam, quæ ad propositum nostrum (id autem est, vt Operi nonnihil lucis adferamus) videbuntur sufficere: reliquaeque ex ijs, quos dixi petantur libris. Primò, quòd in Operis inscriptione posuimus, M. ANTONINI PHILOSOPHI: cognomentum in Græco non erat additum. est autem cuitandæ obscuritatis causa à nobis adiectum. Duo enim fuere Antonini Imperatores, quorum alter Pius, alter Philosophus cognominatus est. Scriptum esse hoc opus à posteriore, cum plurimis aliis argumentis, quæ in promtu sit ex vtriusq; historia colligere, tum Suidæ testimonio constat. eius hæc sunt verba in vocabulo μάρτῡρ · ἔτ̄ ἐγραψε τὰ ἰδία διαγωγὴν βιβλίοις ιϚ[?]. Hoc est : Scripsit hic de vita sua libros duodecim. Quod idem est cum inscriptione nostra, ἐν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ βιβλίῳ ιϚ[?].
units.tr: It was written by the Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Verus, the one who bore the surname Philosopher. His life survives, written out by our Dio and inserted in the epitome of Xiphilinus, and it is also treated by Julius Capitolinus and others. I will adduce only those points that seem sufficient for my purpose, which is to shed some light on the Work, and the rest may be sought in the books I have mentioned. First, in the title of the Work we have put "M. ANTONINUS PHILOSOPHUS"; the surname was not added in the Greek, and we have added it to avoid confusion. There were two Emperors named Antoninus, one surnamed Pius and the other Philosopher. That this work was written by the latter is established by many other arguments, which can readily be drawn from the history of both, and by the testimony of Suidas. His words under the word μάρτυρ are: "He also wrote twelve books about his own life" [ἔτ̄ ἐγραψε τὰ ἰδία διαγωγὴν βιβλίοις ιϚ]. That is: "He wrote twelve books about his own life," which is the same as our title, "In his own book, XII" [ἐν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ βιβλίῳ ιϚ].

units.la: Operæprecium porrò esse arbitror, nonnihil de genere & affinitatibus eius commemorare: quando ipse libro primo suorum familiarium mentionem facit. Adrianus Imperator, cum liberos nullos suscepisset, adoptauit L. Ceionium Commodum Verum, cui ea ex adoptione Aelij & Cæsaris cognomina obtigerunt. Hic vivente etiamnum Adriano decessit vita, filio ciusdem eiusdem nominis relicto. Itaq; Adrianus ut successorem dignum relinqueret reipub. T. Aurelium Fulvium Antoninum (qui & successit ipsi, & Pius est cognominatus) adoptavit: adoptandosq; ei praeterea dedit Veri, quem diximus, superstitem filium, & M. Antoninum, qui deinde Philosophus est appellatus. Erat hic (uti mox demonstrabimus) necessitate iu[?]stus T. Aurelio Antonino. Uterq; defuncto Antonino Pio, summae rerum praefuit: donec L. Verus, L. F. rebus bellicis egregie gestis, bello Marcomannico apud Altinum apoplexia vitam claudens, Antonino Philosopho imperium collega vacuum reliquit.
units.tr: I think it worth while to say something further about his family and connections, since he himself mentions his relatives and close associates in the first book. The Emperor Hadrian, having no children, adopted Lucius Ceionius Commodus Verus, who received on that adoption the names Aelius and Caesar. He died while Hadrian was still alive, leaving a son of the same name. So that Hadrian might leave a worthy successor to the state, he adopted Titus Aurelius Fulvius Antoninus, who succeeded him and was surnamed Pius; and he also gave them to be adopted, besides the surviving son of Verus just mentioned, Marcus Antoninus, who was afterwards called Philosopher. This Marcus was (as I shall show presently) by necessity a relative of Titus Aurelius Antoninus. After Antoninus Pius died, both of them held the highest power, until Lucius Verus, son of Lucius, having conducted the wars brilliantly, died of apoplexy at Altinum during the Marcomannic war, and left the Emperor Antoninus Philosopher alone in the empire as his colleague.

units.la: Caeterum Antonino Pio uxor fuit Annia Faustina Galeria, filia Annij Veri, clarissimi viri, qui & bis cos. (apud Xiphilinum sub finem Adriani legitur tertium consulatum obtinuisse, haud scio an mendose) & urbis praefectus fuit.
units.tr: Moreover, Antoninus Pius had as his wife Annia Faustina Galeria, daughter of Annius Verus, a most distinguished man, who was twice consul (in Xiphilinus, at the end of Hadrian's reign, he is said to have held a third consulship, which I do not know whether to call a mistake) and was prefect of the city.

units.la: Ac quoniam mentio Xiphilini incidit, obiter annotandum putavi, quod in editione Xiphilini cum Dione nostro editi, eo facilius me fefellerat, quod illum ipse non converteram: ea modo correxi quae erant male interpretata, idq; properas. Nempe ubi est de M. Antonino philosopho, ἀὐτ[?]ὶς βύρα τῆς τρὶς ὑπατεύσαντ[?]ς καὶ χιλιαρχήσαντ[?]ς ἔγγονος[?], & in Latino, Filius Annij Veri, qui III consul, ac tribunus militum fuerat: legendum dis pro τρὶς, ut dixi, videri ex Capitolino posse. Certe χιλιαρχήσαντ[?]ος, non χιλιαρχήσαντ[?]ος debere scribi: porro Latine legendum nepo (hoc enim est ἔγγονος) Annij Veri, qui III. consul, & praefectus urbis fuerat. Ita Capitolinus habet, & consentaneum est rationi. Enimuero Annius iste Verus, auus paternus fuit M. Antonini Philosophi. Habuit enim filium Annium Verum, qui in praetura obijt. eius uxor fuit Domitia Caluilla, Caluisij Tulli bis Consulis filia. His natus fuit M. Antoninus Philosophus, qui etiam Catilij cognomen tulit, à proauo materno. Porrò habuit M. Antoninus Philosophus in matrimonio Faustinam, T. Antonini Pij, & amitae suae Annia Faustinae Galeriae filiam. Suam autem filiam Lucillam L. Vero collegae nuptum dedit.
units.tr: Since mention of Xiphilinus has come up, I thought it worth noting in passing that I had been misled more easily in the edition of Xiphilinus published with our Dio, since I had not translated him myself. I have corrected only those passages that were badly translated, and that hastily. Namely, where it is said of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher: "son of Annius Verus, of the grandson [ἔγγονος] of the man who was thrice consul and tribune of soldiers" [ἀὐτ̄ὶς βύρα τῆς τρὶς ὑπατεύσαντ̄ς καὶ χιλιαρχήσαντ̄ς ἔγγονος], and in the Latin, "son of Annius Verus, who was consul for the third time and tribune of the soldiers," it seems from Capitolinus that the word for "thrice" should be read differently, as I have said. Certainly χιλιαρχήσαντος should be written, not χιλιαρχήσαντος. Further, in Latin one should read "grandson" (for this is ἔγγονος) "of Annius Verus, who was consul for the third time and prefect of the city." So Capitolinus has it, and it agrees with reason. Indeed this Annius Verus was the paternal grandfather of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher. For he had a son, Annius Verus, who died while a praetor; this man's wife was Domitia Calvilla, daughter of Calvisius Tullus, twice consul. To them was born Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, who also bore the surname Catilius from his maternal great-grandfather. Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher also had as his wife Faustina, daughter of Titus Antoninus Pius and of his aunt Annia Faustina Galeria. He gave his own daughter Lucilla in marriage to his colleague Lucius Verus.

units.la: Hoc addendum. An. V. C. DCCCCXII, à nato autem Seruatore nostro CLXII, Antoninum Philosophum occepisse imperium.
units.tr: This should be added: in the year of the city 912, and in the 162nd year after our Saviour's birth, Antoninus the Philosopher began his reign.

units.la: Ab auo meo Vero didici.) παρὰ τ̄ πάππᾳ Οὐήρᾳ. Verbū ἐμάθον, aut aliquid tale, subintelligitur: idemq; in omnibus sequentibus particulis. Ego addendū de meo singulis periodis aliquod verbum censui. Nam (nisi fallor) voluit hoc libro ostendere, qua potissimum in re singulos suorum cum necessariorum, tum familiariū admiratus, imitatusq; esset.
units.tr: "I learnt from my grandfather Verus" [παρὰ τῷ πάππῳ Οὐήρῳ]. The verb "I learnt" or something similar is to be understood, and the same with all the following clauses. I thought I should add some word of my own to each sentence. For (unless I am mistaken) in this book he wished to show in what particular respects he most admired and imitated each of his relatives and close associates.

units.la: 1 Ne auriga prasinus.) Quatuor genera fuerunt aurigarum apud Romanos, distincta coloribus, albo, rufo, prasino (qui est porraceus, nimirum viridis) & veneto. Patet hoc ex Dionis Nerone.
units.tr: 1 "Not a green charioteer." There were four kinds of charioteers among the Romans, distinguished by colours: white, red, green (prasinus, that is leek-green, namely green) and blue (veneta). This is clear from Dio's Nero.

units.la: A' Diogneto.) Operam praeterea pingendo sub magistro Diogeneto (forte Diogneto)dedit. Iulius Capitolinus.
units.tr: "From Diognetus." He also practised painting under a teacher, Diogenetus (perhaps Diognetus). Julius Capitolinus.

units.la: Neq; animi causa coturnices.) ὀρτυγοτροφίαν. Hæc ipsa verba sunt apud Suidam in voce ὀρτυγοκόπων[?]: non tamen explicata. Ludi quidem genus ibi describit, in quo coturnices in gyrum collocatæ percuterentur, &c. Citatq; locos è Platone, illius ludicri mentionem continentes. Existimo igitur τῆς ὀρτυγοτροφίας, aut ὀρτυγοκοπίας verbo prouerbialiter omnia ludicra, & inania exercitia autores intellexisse. Vide Plutarchum de audiendis poëtis, & ibi à nobis indicata.
units.tr: "Nor for amusement, quails." [ὀρτυγοτροφίαν]. These are the very words in Suidas under the word ὀρτυγοκόπων, but they are not explained there. There he describes a kind of game in which quails placed in a circle are struck, and so on; and he cites passages from Plato that mention that game. I therefore think that the authors understood by the phrase "quail-rearing" or "quail-fighting" proverbially all frivolous games and empty exercises. See Plutarch, On Listening to Poets, and the notes I have given there.

units.la: De contemplationibus.) περὶ θεωρημάτων[?] qualia sunt in physicis, ac præsertim mathematicis, vbi nullus vsus, & effectio, sed cognitio tantum requiritur.
units.tr: "On contemplations." [περὶ θεωρημάτων], such as occur in natural philosophy, and especially in mathematics, where no use or effect is required, only knowledge.

units.la: Exercitijs dediti, ac laboriosi.) τὸν ἀσκητικόν, ἢ τὸν συσφαιρητικόν, forte συσφαιρητικόν. Sensui tamen videor consuluisse.
units.tr: "Devoted to exercises and laborious." [τὸν ἀσκητικόν, ἢ τὸν συσφαιρητικόν], perhaps συσφαιρητικόν. Yet I think I have kept to the sense.

units.la: Et Astrologia.) In Græco quidem est ἀστρολογίας: quod est, facetijs, & vrbanitate in dicendo. Ego tamen ἀστρολογίας legi ac verti: nam videtur loqui de disciplinis istis, quæ eo nomine male audiebant, quòd plus ostentationis & inanis studij ac laboris, quàm fructus & verę vtilitatis haberent: in quibus numeratam fuisse ἀστρολογίαν, & adhuc à doctis multis numerari, satis notum est. Nunc sane ἀργολογίαν[?] retinerem, & nimis exquisitæ in dicendo venustatis affectatum studium, (<bl>wort gebreng</bl>) intelligerem. quod neq; decet magnos viros, & sæpe de elegantibus ridiculos facit.
units.tr: "And astrology." In the Greek it is [ἀστρολογίας], which means "wit and urbanity in speaking." I, however, read and translated ἀστρολογίας, for he seems to be speaking of those disciplines which had a bad name under that title, because they had more show and empty study and labour than real fruit and usefulness. That astrology was counted among such things, and still is by many learned men, is well enough known. Indeed I would now keep "idle talk" [ἀργολογίαν] and understand it as an affectation of over-refined elegance in speech (<bl>wort gebreng</bl>). This neither becomes great men, nor often makes them ridiculous over matters of taste.

units.la: Alloquio facilitatem )Legitur enim συλλαλέντως. Atqui ego nunc lego συλλαλλέντως: versio nec sic quidem male congruit. Post περιλαλᾶν, alios deferre, de aliis male loqui intelligo. forte scripserat περὶ ἄλλων, aut περὶ αὐτὸν λαλεῖν, ut ij intelligantur qui sese prædicant.
units.tr: "Affability in address." For the Greek is read as συλλαλέντως. But I now read συλλαλλέντως, and the translation fits this reading well enough. After περιλαλᾶν, I understand "to carry tales about others, to speak ill of others." Perhaps he had written περὶ ἄλλων, or περὶ αὐτὸν λαλεῖν, so that it would mean those who boast of themselves.

units.la: 6 Certamq; constantiam.) ἀναμφιβόλως ἀκύβευτον[?]. Cubus alioquin constantiæ signum est apud philosophos: ideoq; in Timæo Platonis cubo terra confertur, ut elementorum stabilissimum. Sed quia tesseris luditur, ac multiplices sunt, varijq; casus: ea ratione inconstantiæ τὸ κυβευτὸν tribuitur: ut sit ἀκύβευτον, quod constanter persistit, neq; facile movetur aut circumvoluitur. Itaque etiam D. Paulus monet, ut κυβείας τὴν ἀνθρώπων caveamus: hoc est, ne omni vento doctrinæ circumagi nos, & in errores abripi patiamur.
units.tr: 6 "And steadfast constancy." [ἀναμφιβόλως ἀκύβευτον]. Among philosophers the cube is otherwise a sign of constancy; therefore in Plato's Timaeus earth is compared to the cube, as the most stable of the elements. But because dice are played with tesserae, which are many-sided and have varied throws, gambling [τὸ κυβευτὸν] is for this reason ascribed to inconstancy; so that ἀκύβευτον means what persists steadily and is not easily moved or turned about. Accordingly St Paul also warns us to beware of the trickery [κυβείας] of men: that is, not to let ourselves be carried about by every wind of doctrine and dragged into error.

units.la: In Sexto.) Ἕσξτ[?], lego Σέξτ. Sextus philosophus, quo usus est plurimum Antoninus, fuit patria Chæronensis, nepos Plutarchi.
units.tr: "In Sextus." [Ἕσξτ̄]; I read Σέξτ̄. Sextus the philosopher, whom Antoninus used very much, was a native of Chaeronea, and a grandson of Plutarch.

units.la: 8 Erga priuatos.) Quod in Græco sequitur, καὶ τὸ ἀθεώρητον τῶν διοπτευόντων, convertissem, si intellexissem. Malui itaq; asterisco notare, quàm arroganter aliquid facere. Suspicor velle eum loqui de
units.tr: 8 "Towards private persons." What follows in the Greek, [καὶ τὸ ἀθεώρητον τῶν διοπτευόντων], I would have translated if I had understood it. I preferred to mark it with an asterisk rather than to do something arrogant. I suspect he means to speak of
φ 5 freedom from the vanity of pride and arrogance.

units.la: 9 Per eundem cognoui Thraseam.) Egregia virtutum ac constantiæ exempla. De Thrasea est apud Tacitum, Dionem, Suetoniumq;ut & de Heluidio. Reliquorum vitæ sunt apud Plutarchū.
units.tr: 9 "Through the same person I came to know Thrasea." These are outstanding examples of virtue and constancy. Thrasea is mentioned in Tacitus, Dio and Suetonius, as also Helvidius. The lives of the others are in Plutarch.

units.la: Adulationem compescebat. ) ἐπ' αὐτῇ γαλλῶσα. Credo scriptum fuisse συγαλλῶσα.
units.tr: He checked flattery. [ἐπ' αὐτῇ γαλλῶσα]. I believe it was written συγαλλῶσα.

units.la: Quippe vir quid ex visu.) καὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις ἀνθρώποις, vitiose: lego, καὶ τῶις τοιούτοις, καὶ ἀνθρώπου.
units.tr: Indeed, a man from what he saw. The reading καὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις ἀνθρώποις is faulty; I read καὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις, καὶ ἀνθρώπου.

units.la: 10 Non vtebatur alieno tempore.) Diuinauit hoc loco, (ἐν εὐ ἀωρεὶ λέγης, quod est forte ἀπὸ λέω.) sicut & in sequenti periodo: vbi quidem pro τόπῳ, τρόπῳ legi. & vbi est, Ad sudorem vsque, suspectum habeo: sunt enim salebrosa hæc.
units.tr: 10 He did not use an unseasonable time. I guessed at this point (ἐν εὐ ἀωρεὶ λέγης, which is perhaps from λέω), as also in the following period, where I read τρόπῳ for τόπῳ. Where it says "to the point of sweating," I hold it suspect, for these words are rough and obscure.

units.la: 11 Sicut Chrefæ.) ὡσαύτως χρήσει. Soleo asterisco notare, quæ manca suspicer. Forte est, Quomodo vtaris χρήσει. mutilus est locus.
units.tr: 11 As for Chrefes. [ὡσαύτως χρήσει]. I am accustomed to mark with an asterisk what I suspect to be missing. Perhaps it is "how you use" [χρήσει]. The passage is mutilated.

units.la: Hæc in Quadis.) Puto solitū annotare, quibus in locis singula esset commentatus. Sic ad finem libri secundi est, Carnunti ea esse scripta. Sequentia cum prioribus non cohærent.
units.tr: These things among the Quadi. I think he was accustomed to note in which places each piece had been studied. So at the end of the second book is "that these were written at Carnuntum." The following does not cohere with what precedes.

units.la: 1 Et hic initium videtur deesse, & vbi est ἡ χρῆ αὐτοῦς: nihil adest, ad quod illud αὐτοῦς referri possit. Cæterum verbo ἀπαθρεᾶσθαι vsus est metaphoricè. Suidas enim & alij docent, id esse, pulsis nubibus bus serenitatem facere.
units.tr: 1 And here the beginning seems to be missing, and where it reads ἡ χρῆ αὐτοῦς, there is nothing to which that αὐτοῦς could refer. Moreover, he used the verb ἀπαθρεᾶσθαι metaphorically. For Suidas and others teach that it means to drive away the clouds and make the sky clear.

units.la: 2 Si quis eatenus eius suauitatem.) τὸ νόστιμον est in Graeco, quod vocabulum dulcedinem significat. νόστος enim est reditus in patriam, qua nihil esse dulcius, Homerici Vlyssis testimonio receptum est. Et cum Homerus νόστον vocet μελιηδέα: inde factum est, ut dulcia vocentur νοστίμα, ut Eustathius docet: καὶ νόστῳ ὁμοιοῦσθαι ἡ ἡδύτης. Vtitur eodem modo Lucianus πρὸς τὸν ... [illegible, ~10 letters] ... τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐπὶ τὴν [?] ... ὡς τὸ μὲν νομιμώτατον τὴν παρεισπνυσαμένων ὁ νέπνος [?] ... ἄνω εἰς τὸν ἀέρα οἴχεται.
units.tr: 2 If anyone so far enjoys its sweetness.) The Greek has τὸ νόστιμον, a word meaning sweetness or charm. For νόστος is a return to one's homeland, and the testimony of Homer's Ulysses has established that nothing is sweeter. Since Homer calls the return "honey-sweet" [μελιηδέα], it came about that sweet things are called νόστιμα, as Eustathius teaches, and that sweetness is likened to a homecoming. Lucian uses it in the same way: … [the rest of this Greek is too garbled to render with confidence] … the breath goes off up into the air.

units.la: Anima vaga est.) ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ ῥεμβός. Est autem altera lectio annotata ῥεμβός, quam probaui, & secutus sum: neq; enim videtur philosophicum esse, animam rhombo (quae est figura quatuor aequalium laterum, non tamen rectangula) comparari. At ῥεμβὸς vagus est, & ῥεμβεῖσθαι vagari, & incuriè rebus vti, quo vocabulo ipse supra vsus est sub initium libri huius: ὡς καὶ πλανᾶσθαι ῥεμβόμενον, ac vagari desine. Plutarchus Pompeio, ῥεμβόμενον ἐν τοῖς πράγμασι τὴν προσπέτειαν καταμαθών: animaduertens Perpennam vagari, & incuriè rem gerere. Idem in Fabio, ῥεμβόμενον ἀπὸ τῆς πραγματείας, qui saepe à castris aberat vagans alio, ad scortum nimirum suum commeans identidè. Idem in lib.de Communibus notitijs, plane sic est vsus, vt hic nostr. νήφων γὰρ εἰς ἀγελαῖα, ἀλλὰ ῥεμβόμεθα πάντες ἀχνμονοῦν[τες] τὲς [?] ἡμᾶς κακοδαιμονοῦντες [?]. Porro autem adiectiuu̅s masculini generis, substantiuis fœmininis addi Græco more, non est inusitatum: suntq; multa à Budæo annotata eius rei exempla.
units.tr: Anima vaga est.) The Greek has ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ ῥεμβός. There is another reading noted in the margin, ῥεμβός, which I have approved and followed, since it does not seem philosophical to compare the soul to a rhombus, a figure with four equal sides but not right-angled. But ῥεμβὸς means wandering, and ῥεμβεῖσθαι means to wander and to handle affairs carelessly, a word he himself used above at the beginning of this book: "as also to wander astray, and stop wandering." Plutarch, in the Life of Pompey: noticing that Perpenna was wandering and carrying out affairs carelessly, ῥεμβόμενον ἐν τοῖς πράγμασι. The same in the Life of Fabius: ῥεμβόμενον ἀπὸ τῆς πραγματείας, of one who was often away from the camp, wandering elsewhere and going, no doubt, to his mistress. The same in the book On Common Notions he uses it just as our author does here: νήφων γὰρ εἰς ἀγελαῖα … ἀλλὰ ῥεμβόμεθα πάντες … Moreover, an adjective of masculine gender added to feminine substantives in the Greek manner is not unusual, and Budaeus has noted many examples of this.

units.la: In somnij & fumi.) ὑνεφῷ καὶ τύφῳ. Scio τύφον esse fastu, superbiamq; inane: sed ea significatio huc non quadrat. Verti ergo fumum: id enim videtur τύφῳ proprie significare, seu caliginem ab igne proficiscentem: cui vana elatio animi atq; fastus quu fit similimus, commodissima translatione τύφῳ Græcis dicitur, ac definitur ἀναθυμίασις καπνώδης ἐν ἐγ[?]γὺς [?] πυρότης. Ignis non fit sine fumo. Frequenter autem res leues ac fluxæ fumo comparantur. atq; in psalmo etiam Dauidis est: Sicut fumus dies mei. Cæterū, & si non recordor τύφον me pro fumo legisse: tamen id quod dixi, verbo τύφειν satis testatum relinquitur, cuius est apud poetas Græcos usus. Adducam unum exemplum quod in præsentia succurrit, ex Apollon. ἀργοναυτικῶν β.
units.tr: In dream and smoke.) The Greek has ὑνεφῷ καὶ τύφῳ. I know that τύφος means pride and empty conceit, but that sense does not fit here, so I have translated "smoke." For τύφῳ seems properly to mean smoke, or the mist that rises from a fire. Vain elation of spirit and pride is very like this, and so by a most fitting transfer the Greeks call it τύφος, defining it as a smoky exhalation with a fiery heat. Fire is not made without smoke, and light and fleeting things are often compared to smoke, as in the psalm of David: "My days are like smoke." Moreover, although I do not recall having read τύφος for smoke, what I have said is sufficiently attested by the verb τύφειν, which Greek poets use. I will adduce one example that comes to mind at present, from Apollonius, Argonautica book 2.

units.la: Ἐπὶπρὸ δὲ λιγυνόεντιΚαπνῷ τυφόμενοι ωέτρης ἑναὶς ἀϊσσοσι [?].
units.tr: Ἐπὶ πρὸ δὲ λιγυνόεντι καπνῷ τυφόμενοι … [Greek verse, garbled in the scan; it describes bees smouldering in the shrill smoke and rushing out].

units.la: De apibus loquitur. Ibi Scholiastes: καπνῷ τυφόμενοι, αὐτὶ τῆς καπνιζόμενοι. (& sic paulo supra exposuerat τὸ τυφόμενοι) σημαίνει δὲ καὶ τὸ καπνιζόμενον. Si cui tamen hoc non probatur, is pro fumo manem ostentationem aut fastum reponat.
units.tr: He is speaking of bees. There the Scholiast says: καπνῷ τυφόμενοι, instead of καπνιζόμενοι (and so a little above he had explained τὸ τυφόμενοι), and it also means "smoked." If anyone nevertheless does not approve of this, let him put manifest display or pride in place of "smoke."

units.la: Carnunti.) Vrbs Pannoniæ fuit, olim celeberrima, hodie (ut existimatur) Passaw.
units.tr: Carnuntum.) This was a city of Pannonia, once very famous, today (as is thought) Passau.

units.la: 1 Tempus sit vitam relinquendi.) ἐξαντίον αὐτὸν. Est autem ἀπάγειν ἑαυτὸν, sibi ipsi mortem cōscīscere, apud Graecos scriptores. Quae significatio quia huc parum quadrare videbatur, mollioribus usus sum verbis.
