units.tr: 1 It is time to leave life.) [ἐξαντίον αὐτὸν]. Among Greek writers, however, ἀπάγειν ἑαυτὸν means to bring about one's own death. Since that sense seemed to fit poorly here, I have used milder words.

units.la: 2 Oliuis maturisimis.) In Graeco legitur ἀρυπέπισι, scribendum ἀρυπεπέσι. Sed potest ἀρυπέ-τεσι legi (quae lectio erat in margine annotata) ut sint oliuae prae maturitate iam de arbore decidentes: quarum similitudine usus est infra Libro quarto.
units.tr: 2 Very ripe olives.) The Greek reads ἀρυπέπισι; it should be written ἀρυπεπέσι. But it may be read ἀρυπέτεσι (which reading was noted in the margin), so that the olives are already falling from the tree because of overripeness. He used this likeness below in Book Four.

units.la: Leonis supercil.) ἐπισπωύιον. Scholiast. Homeri exponit τὸ συνοφρύωμα τ̄ μετώπᾳ, quod est, superciliorum in fronte commissuram: aitque hinc verbum σνύζεσθαι, quod est irasci, deductum. Nam Homerus leonem iratū describens, Ilia. ρ. ita habet: Γαρ δὲ τ' ἐπισπωύιον κάτω ἕλκετω ὀσσε καλυπ-τῷ. Vide Eustathium.
units.tr: The lion's brow.) ἐπισπωύιον. The Scholiast on Homer explains it as τὸ συνοφρύωμα τῆς μετώπης, that is, the joining of the eyebrows on the forehead, and says that the verb σνύζεσθαι, to be angry, is derived from it. For Homer, describing a lion in a rage in the Iliad (book ρ), has: "and he drew down his brows over his eyes." See Eustathius.

units.la: 3 Castis oculis.) Secus quam Sophocl. qui apud Ciceronem a Pericle reprehenditur ob formam pueri laudatam, quod oculos abstinentes non haberet. 1. Officior.
units.tr: 3 Chaste eyes.) Not as Sophocles, who in Cicero is rebuked by Pericles for praising a boy's beauty, on the ground that he did not have eyes that abstain (from looking). Cicero, De Officiis book 1.

units.la: 4 Democritum pediculi.) Non memini me hunc exitum Democriti legere apud ullum idoneum autorem. de Pherecyde quidem Syro Philosopho legitur. forte est lapsus memoria. et quod est Σωηράτλυ ἄλλοι φθάρτες, falsum est. Ego historiam secutus sum.
units.tr: 4 Democritus died of lice.) I do not remember reading this death of Democritus in any reliable author. It is indeed recorded of Pherecydes the Syrian philosopher that he died of lice. Perhaps this is a lapse of memory. And the statement about Socrates, that "others say" he died of lice, is false. I have followed the story.

units.la: 5 Declinanda est vanitas.) περιΐσταδ. ἀτϙ[?] haud scio, an in hac significatione usi sint Graeci autores antiqui. Pro fugere & declinare etiam D. Paulus usurpavit, ad Timotheum poster.cap.2. τᾶς[?] ἀβεβήλους κενοφωνίας περιΐσταο[?].
units.tr: 5 Vanity must be avoided.) περιΐσταδ. I am not sure whether the ancient Greek authors used it in this sense. St. Paul also used it, in the sense of fleeing and avoiding, in his second letter to Timothy, chapter 2: "avoid profane and empty babblings" [τὰς βεβήλους κενοφωνίας περιΐστασο].

units.la: 6 A temeritate alieni.) ἀπροπηωσίαν[?], vacuitate temeritatis. προπηωσίαν[?] enim προπέτεαν dicit: Sic infra libro XXIIII. ἀπρόπλωτος[?] est, circunspectus, non temerarius.
units.tr: 6 Free from rashness.) ἀπροπηωσίαν, vacancy from rashness. For he says προπέτεια (προπηωσία). Thus below in Book 24, ἀπρόπλωτος means circumspect, not rash.

units.la: 7 Itaque ad finem.) εἰς τέλος[?]: lego εἰς τέλος[?].
units.tr: 7 And so to the end.) εἰς τέλος: I read it as εἰς τέλος.

units.la: Androgynis.) Hoc est, iis qui ambiguo (ut Livius loquitur) inter marem & feminam sexu sunt nati. Graecum retinui, quia est & appositum, & Latinis autoribus, ipsiq; Ciceroni etiam usurpatum: alias Hermaphroditos vocat.
units.tr: Androgynes.) That is, those born with a sex ambiguous (as Livy puts it) between male and female. I have kept the Greek, [ἀνδρόγυνοι], because it fits well and Latin authors, even Cicero himself, have used it; elsewhere he calls them hermaphrodites.

units.la: Nihil non turpe.) Desunt haec in Graeco.
units.tr: Nothing that is not shameful.) These words are absent from the Greek.

units.la: 1 Cum exceptione quadam.) Nimirum ut agat, quantum homini fatum & res permittit proposita. μετ' ὑπεξαιρέσεως[?]. Porro ὑπεξαίρεσιν[?] recte verti exceptionem, ut ex loco Plutarchi patet in vita Numae, ubi scribit, quorundam sententia pontifices à potentia seu potestate denominatos, quod vocabulum haberet vim exceptionis (ὑπεξαιρέσεσιν[?] ibi leges) indicandae: quod scilicet pontisex rem sacram, quantum eius omnino fieri posset, perageret: nec ei fraudi esset, si grave aliquod impedimentum incidisset, quo minus sacra perpetraret.
units.tr: 1 With a certain exception.) Doubtless, that he act as far as fate and the circumstances set before a man allow. μετ' ὑπεξαιρέσεως[?]. Moreover, ὑπεξαίρεσιν[?] is rightly rendered "exception", as is clear from the passage of Plutarch in the Life of Numa, where he writes that, in the opinion of some, pontiffs were named from potentia or potestas, since the word had the force of an exception (there he refers to the laws ὑπεξαιρέσεσιν[?]), indicating that the pontiff would carry out the sacred duty as fully as could be done, and that it would not count against him if some serious hindrance arose that kept him from completing the rites.

units.la: Ad mentem eam quae est reliquarum origo.) λόγῳ ἀσωματικόν[?]. paulò infrà clarius dicet de hoc.
units.tr: To that mind which is the origin of the rest.) λόγῳ ἀσωματικόν[?]. He speaks more clearly of this a little further on.

units.la: Ac qui secundum bonum.) κατὰ τὸν ἀγαθόν. Forte Ἀγάθωνα, quod maximè videtur confirmare articulum τὸν masculinum: & verba quae sequuntur, omnino videntur ex aliquo poëta desumpta. Agathonem verò fuisse poëtam, satis constat ex multis scriptoribus idoneis: citaturq; eius versus ab ipso Aristotele, lib. πρώτῳ Νικομ. 6. Porrò quid sit μέλαν ὠδήν, nigri morcs[?], infrà ipse describit.
units.tr: And he who according to the good.) κατὰ τὸν ἀγαθόν. Perhaps it is Ἀγάθωνα, which especially seems to confirm the masculine article τὸν; and the words that follow seem altogether taken from some poet. That Agathon was a poet is fairly well established by many reliable writers, and his verse is cited by Aristotle himself in book 1 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 6. Moreover, what "black song" (μέλαν ὠδήν) is, he describes further below.

units.la: Nisi ratione cuiusdam dispensationis.) Locus est depravatus, atq; ideo obscurus.
units.tr: Unless by reason of some dispensation.) The passage is corrupt, and therefore obscure.

units.la: Nihil eo plus confert.) μήποτε ἀμαυρὸν τ' ἀναγκαῖα. Nisi fallor, sensus ipse ostendit esse legendum, μηδ' ἀμαυρὸν τ.
units.tr: Nothing contributes more to this.) μήποτε ἀμαυρὸν τ' ἀναγκαῖα. Unless I am mistaken, the sense itself shows that μηδ' ἀμαυρὸν τ. should be read.

units.la: Eius quoq; exemplum recolendum.) Haec comparatio est interpolata, nec cohaerent inter se quae sequuntur.
units.tr: His example too is to be recalled.) This comparison is interpolated, and what follows does not hang together.

units.la: Non tàquam si dormitemus.) Sensus est: Perficiendum strenuè, quod recto consilio agendum suscepe-rimus: neque in medio actu desistendum, aut titubandum. Nam in somnis saepe imaginamur nobis aliquid agere, nihil tamen efficimus, sed (ut pulcerrimè expressit Maro)
units.tr: Not as if we were sleeping.) The sense is: what we have undertaken to do on sound judgement must be carried through vigorously, and one must not give up or falter in the middle of the action. For in dreams we often imagine ourselves doing something, yet achieve nothing; but (as Maro expressed most beautifully)

units.la: In medijs conatibus ægri Succidimus, non lingua valet, non corpore notæ Sufficiunt vires, nec vox, aut verba sequuntur.
units.tr: In the midst of our efforts we sick men collapse; the tongue has no strength, the familiar powers of the body fail, and neither voice nor words follow.

units.la: Quot vrbes mortuæ.) Ita Seruius Sulpitius in cōsolatoria ad M. Tullium epistola, de Corintho, Athenis & Megaris loquitur: Quum vno loco tot vrbium cadauera proiecta iaceant.
units.tr: How many cities dead.) Thus Servius Sulpicius, in his letter of consolation to M. Tullius, speaks of Corinth, Athens and Megara: When in one place so many corpses of cities lie cast forth.

units.la: Helice.) Vrbs fuit Achaiæ, in sinu Corinthiaco sita. Hanc a mari absorpta testatur Polyb. lib. 2. Plin. nat. hist. li. 2. cap. 92. & Ouid. 15. Metamorph.
units.tr: Helice.) It was a city of Achaea, situated on the Corinthian gulf. Polybius, book 2, attests that it was swallowed up by the sea, as do Pliny, Natural History, book 2, chapter 92, and Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.

units.la: Si quæras Helicen, & Burin, Achaidas vrbes, Inuenies sub aquis, &c.
units.tr: If you seek Helice and Buris, the Achaean cities, you will find them under the waters, etc.

units.la: Pompeij & Herculanum oppida fuerunt Campaniæ, haud procul a Vesuvio monte: vt Plin. oftend-d' lib. 3. cap. 5. quorum de interitu nihil habeo copertum, nisi forte conflagratione Vesuvij montis (quæ accidit Titi Vespasiani ætate, & in eius vita a Dione describitur) pericrint. fit quidem etiam infra lib. 8. Pompeiorum interitus mentio.
units.tr: Pompeii and Herculaneum were towns of Campania, not far from Mount Vesuvius, as Pliny shows in book 3, chapter 5. I have nothing certain about their destruction, unless perhaps they perished in the conflagration of Mount Vesuvius (which happened in the age of Titus Vespasian and is described by Dio in his life). Indeed, a mention of the destruction of Pompeii is also made further on, in book 8.

units.la: Quod heri fuit piscis.) In Graeco est μυξάζειν[?] ... piscem aliquem innui, ex eo quòd [illegible, ~6 letters] sequitur, coniicio: certi nihil habeo.
units.tr: What was yesterday a fish.) In the Greek it is μυξάζειν[?] ... I conjecture that some fish is meant, from what follows [illegible, about six letters]; I have nothing certain.

units.la: Similis esse debes promotorii.) Hac similitudine[?] Cicero eleganter usus est, ad Papirium Pætum scribens de fortuna: Quam existimo leuem & imbecillem, ab animo firmo & graui, tanquam fluctum a saxo frangi oportere.
units.tr: You should be like a promontory.) Cicero used this comparison elegantly in writing to Papirius Paetus about fortune: that fortune, which I think is light and feeble, ought to be broken by a firm and serious mind, as a wave is broken by a rock.

units.la: Indignari cunctari.) γλισχρὸν ἐστι λεπτόν[?], tenax. itaq; supra ad finem libri prioris, γλίχρως ἐνδιαβιβᾶν τῷ ἡ̃ν[?] dixit diu viuere. ucre. Quare hic γλιχροῦντες[?] vertendum putaui, cunctari: hoc est, ægre ac nulla cum alacritate suum officium facere. quod vitium supra etiam damnauit.
units.tr: To be reluctant, to dawdle.) γλισχρὸν ἐστι λεπτόν[?], tenacious. Therefore above, at the end of the previous book, he said γλίχρως ἐνδιαβιβᾶν τῷ ἡ̃ν[?], to live long. Hence here I thought γλιχροῦντες[?] should be rendered "to dawdle", that is, to perform one's duty with difficulty and no alacrity. This fault he also condemned above.

units.la: 2 Leuem esse.) προπετεῖν[?]: ἢ προπέτειαν, βλακείαν καὶ προπέτειαν[?], hoc est, stultam et inanem temeritatem, seu leuitatem, vbi non vt ex vsu est, sed ostentationis vanæ gratia quicquam agitur. D. Paulus 1. Corint. 13. ἡ ἀγάπη οὐ περπερεύεται[?]: Charitas non est leuis, aut nugax.
units.tr: 2 Lightness.) προπετεῖν[?]: ἢ προπέτειαν, βλακείαν καὶ προπέτειαν[?], that is, foolish and empty rashness or levity, where something is done not as is useful but for the sake of vain display. St Paul, 1 Corinthians 13: ἡ ἀγάπη οὐ περπερεύεται[?]: Charity is not frivolous or trifling.

units.la: 3 Atheniensium erat hoc votum.) Etsi locus non est plenus, tamen satis apparet eum voluisse improbare commune illud et damnosissimum vitium, quo plerique tantum ea curant, expetunt, et optant, quæ sibi ipsis priuatim prosint: nihil solliciti de communi bono. Id vero vitium, omnium fere quæ sunt in rebus publicis malorum causa est et origo. At plerique hodie tales esse laborant, qui furam quam genu longius abesse dicant, (vt est apud Theocritum) et quorum hoc sit votum, Ἀνδρῶν μοί τι γένοιτο[?], mihi ipsi aliquid boni contingat: secus, quam ab animali ad societatem ciuilem nato fieri debeat. Præclara fuit apud Persas lex ea de re lata, quam Herodotus his verbis refert: ἑαυτὸν μὲν ἀνδρῶν δύο ἰδίῃ μοῦνῳ[?], ἢ οἱ ἐγγινόμενοι ἀγαθά[?]. Ὁ γὰρ ὧν τοῖσι Πέρσῃσι νόμος κατάσχετον ἐν γὰρ τοῖσι ἄπαξι Πέρσῃσι καὶ αὐτὸς γίνεται[?]. Hoc est: Perse, cum rem sacram facit, sibi ipsi priuatim aliquid boni precari religio est. Caeterum omnibus Persis, ac regi, prosperitatem optat: quippe inter uniuersos Persas, ipse quoq; unus est. Et diuina est apud Euripidem Menaecei, se pro patria deuoturi sententia, quam adscribam, ut hic Antonini locus recte intelligatur:
units.tr: 3 The Athenians had this prayer.) Although the passage is not complete, it nonetheless sufficiently appears that he wished to censure that common and most damaging vice, by which most people care for, seek and wish only those things that benefit themselves privately, being not at all anxious about the common good. Indeed, this vice is nearly the cause and origin of almost all the evils in commonwealths. But many today are troubled to be such people, who say that the fox is further away than the knee (as in Theocritus), and whose wish is "that something good may come to me myself", otherwise than should be done by an animal born for civil society. A splendid law on this matter was passed among the Persians, which Herodotus reports in these words: [Herodotus:] a man may not pray for good things for himself alone and privately; for this is the custom of the Persians, that they hold ... among all Persians he too is one. That is: when a Persian performs a sacred rite, it is considered a scruple to pray for some good for himself privately. But he prays for prosperity for all Persians and for the king, since he himself too is one among all the Persians. And there is a divine sentiment in Euripides about Menoeceus, who vows to devote himself for his country, which I will append so that this passage of Antoninus may be rightly understood:

units.la: Εἰ γὰρ λαβὼν ἐναγ-ῳ̂ ὅ, τι ἀμύνατο τῆςΧρησ-τὸν, Ἀιελέοι τῆτο, ἢ ἐις κοινὸν φέρειΠατρίδι, μακὰ ὢν ἂν ἀι πόλεις ἐλασσόνωσιΠεριφύλλαι, τὸ κοινὸν ἀντυχοίην ἂν. id est: Si quilibet, quantum queat boni, lubens Patriae offerat, donetq; publicae rei: Haud totidem euenient ciuitatibus mala, Sed accident in posterum res prosperae.
units.tr: If anyone, as much as he is able, gladly offers good to his country and gives it to the public good, not so many evils will befall the cities, but prosperous things will come in future.

units.la: Itaq; Athenienses iniuste & illiberaliter suis tantum agris pluuiam & fertilitatem poscebant: qui si omnibus hominibus felicitatem ac successa omnia optassent, & humanae rationem societatis habuissent, neq; communi prosperitate exclusi fuissent.
units.tr: And so the Athenians unjustly and illiberally asked for rain and fertility only for their own fields. If they had wished for happiness and success for all men, and had taken account of human fellowship, they would not have been excluded from common prosperity.

units.la: Totum enim mutilatur.) Τὴν ἀ[?]ὰ γὰρ τὸ ὁλόκληρον: non τυφλῶς.
units.tr: For the whole is mutilated.) τὴν ἀ[?]ὰ γὰρ τὸ ὁλόκληρον: not blindly.

units.la: Neq; tibi est ad philosophiam.) Sensus huius loci habet nonnihil obscuritatis. videtur autem haec esse sententia: Si quid instituueris agere secundum rectam rationem, & cuctus consilio tuo non respondeat, non debes idcirco tuum propositum damnare: sed potius cogitare, quam multa in rebus humanis sint, & accidere queant, quae obstent, quo minus nus[?] id quod quæris, consequaris. Itaque conscientia boni propositi, & rationum recte subductarum animus est confirmandus: ferendumque quod sors fert humana, & rerum caducarum conditio. Hæc tibi in promtu sunt habenda, iam multo ante ex philosophia petita, atque ad usum præparata: ne tum demum consilium & præceptu velis petere à philosophia, cum eo sit utendum. est enim hoc parum prudentiæ. Ita qui lippitudine laborant, aut alio morbo, remedia habent præparata & instructa, quibus ingruente malo utantur: non tum demum ea quærunt, aut circumspiciunt, cum eorum usus est. Et in prælio aut dimicatione non emitur, neque acuitur gladius, sed usurpatur. Videturque omnino id velle Antoninus dicere, quod est apud Plutarch. (Probl. Rom. 85.) his verbis: ἀεὶ γὰρ παρασκευασαμένους χρὴ, ἀλλὰ μὴ ἀπαρασκευάστως προσφέροντας· ὡς Μύσων πρὸς Χίλωνα τὸν σοφὸν εἶπεν, ὁ χειμῶνι θέμενος τὴν [illegible, ~8 letters]. Hoc est: Præparatis quæ ex usu sunt, agendum est, non inter agendum præparáda[?] ea quibus opus est: idque Myso Chiloni, ei qui sapiens est usurpatus, dixit, hyeme ventilabrum fabricans.
units.tr: Nor is it for philosophy.) The sense of this passage has some obscurity. The meaning seems to be this: if you have set out to act according to right reason, and the outcome does not correspond to your plan, you must not on that account condemn your purpose; rather you should consider how many things in human affairs can happen to hinder you from attaining what you seek. Therefore the mind must be strengthened by the consciousness of a good purpose and of reasons rightly reckoned, and must bear what human lot and the condition of transient things bring. These things must be kept ready to hand, already drawn long before from philosophy and prepared for use, so that you do not wish to seek counsel and precepts from philosophy only when you must use them. For that is little wisdom. Thus those who suffer from inflamed eyes or some other illness keep remedies prepared and at hand to use when the evil attacks; they do not seek them out or look around for them only when they need them. And in battle or combat the sword is not sharpened or forged, but used. Antoninus seems entirely to wish to say what is found in Plutarch (Roman Questions 85) in these words: "One must always be prepared, and not approach unprepared; as Myson said to the wise Chilon, when he was making a winnowing-fan in winter." That is: one must act with things that are useful, prepared in advance, not preparing in the midst of action what is needed. And Myson said this to Chilon, who is counted among the wise, while making a winnowing-fan in winter.

units.la: 6 Quod non sub hæc referatur.) Verba in Græco non cohærent. Loqui videtur de vulgi depravato iudicio, ea quæ videntur, neque sunt tamen bona, veris bonis præferenti. Id fit ex imperitia. Idemque accidit his, quod Plato alicubi ex Stesichoro citat: Troianos, cum veram Helenam non cognoscerent, scerent[?], de idolo eius siue imani figura decertasse. Quod idem fabula Ixionis, cum nube, quam Iunonem putabat, concumbentis, Poetæ delineant.
units.tr: 6 That is not referred under these.) The words in the Greek do not cohere. It seems to speak of the corrupted judgement of the crowd, which prefers things that seem good but are not to true goods. This happens through inexperience. The same thing happens to what Plato somewhere cites from Stesichorus: that the Trojans, not recognising the true Helen, fought over her idol or image-like figure. The poets depict the same in the story of Ixion, who lay with a cloud he thought was Juno.

units.la: 7 Ex forma & materia.) Formam dixi, quod autor τὸ αὐτοειδὲς[?] id est, id quod causæ vim & naturam habet. Cæterum materiam, quasi patiendi, formam (quæ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι, εἶδος[?], ἐνέργεια, ἐντελέχεια, philosophis dicitur) agendi & efficiendi vim habere, notum est ex Physicis. Porrò autem de rerum caducarum perpetuitate, quam habent continenti formarum naturalium in materia successione perpetuisque rerum mutationibus, copiosè est ab Aristotele cum alibi, tum in libris de Ortu & interitu disputatum.
units.tr: 7 From form and matter.) I have said "form" because the author calls it [τὸ αὐτοειδές], that is, what has the power and nature of a cause. That matter, as it were the thing that undergoes, and form (which philosophers call [τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι], [εἶδος], [ἐνέργεια], [ἐντελέχεια]) have the power of acting and producing, is known from the Physics. Further, Aristotle has discussed at length the perpetuity of perishable things, which they have through the continuous succession of natural forms in matter and the constant changes of things, both elsewhere and in the books On Generation and Corruption.

units.la: 8 Ratio & rationalis.) Ostendit, in rebus humanis non esse eam, quæ est in scientijs & artibus, certitudinem atque constantiam & perfectionem. Hoc ipsum est quod Aristoteles initio suorum ad Nicomachum Ethicorum, tam accuratè docet atque monet: Non esse eandem quæ est in aliis, in philosophia morali demonstrationum & præceptorum certitudinem requirendam: sed ratione materiæ subiectæ omnia examinanda. Adscribam verba Platonis, eādem rem optimè explanantia, idque Latinè: Dissimilitudines (inquit) cum hominum, tum actionum, rerumque humanarum tanta, ut nihil ferè in hus[?] ne vno quidem momento quiescat ac perstet, inconstantia efficiunt, ne qua de ijs omnibus ars, quae omnibus temporibus congruat, tradi possit. His infert Antoninus: Consequens ergo esse, ut finis hominis non in rebus extra ipsum positis, ac nō vere bonis & mutabilibus collocetur. Quod autem κατορθώσεις[?] rectas effectiones converti, Ciceronem sequutus sum autorem, qui ita extulit libro De finibus bonorum & malorum tertio.
units.tr: 8 Reason and rational.) He shows that in human affairs there is not the certainty, constancy and perfection that belong to the sciences and arts. This is exactly what Aristotle teaches and warns so carefully at the beginning of his Nicomachean Ethics: that in moral philosophy one must not look for the same certainty of demonstrations and precepts as in other fields, but that everything must be judged according to the nature of the subject matter. I will add Plato's words, which explain the same point very well, here in Latin: "The dissimilarities of men, and of their actions and human affairs, produce such inconstancy that scarcely anything rests or abides even for a single moment, so that no art that fits all times can be handed down concerning all these things." To this Antoninus adds: "It follows, therefore, that man's end should not be placed in things outside himself, in things that are not truly good and are changeable." As for [κατορθώσεις], I have followed the author Cicero, who rendered it as "right actions" in the third book of De finibus bonorum et malorum.
9 And that he bear.) [ἀνταντέον]. I read [ἀντιτέον].

units.la: 10 Ei qui hircum olet.) χάσωι est scribendum, non ὀρχάσωι. χάσω ἐστὶ factor ille, qui hirsutis (ut est apud Horatium) cubat grauis hircus in alis. αὐτὸν ἡμῶν τὸ χάσσον ἐξυπομεῖναι[?]. milites Alexandri de Persis, pugnam inituri. Plutarch. Apophtheg.
units.tr: 10 To the man who smells of goat.) It should be written [χάσωι], not [ὀρχάσωι]. The [χάσω] is that foul fellow who lies with hairy armpits, a heavy goat (as in Horace). [αὐτὸν ἡμῶν τὸ χάσσον ἐξυπομεῖναι]: the soldiers of Alexander, about to engage the Persians. Plutarch, Apophthegms.

units.la: 11 Aequum te praebuisti.) ἐς ὅσον δὲ ἀγνώμονας ἀγνώμων ἐγενέσθαι[?]. Ego ἀγνώμων[?] lego. quid enim erat laudis, malis se malum praebuisse? praesertim quum saepius iam monuerit, vitia hominum nobis esse ferenda.
units.tr: 11 You have shown yourself fair.) [ἐς ὅσον δὲ ἀγνώμονας ἀγνώμων ἐγενέσθαι]. I read [ἀγνώμων]. For what praise was there in showing oneself bad to bad men? Especially since he has already warned more than once that we must bear with the vices of men.

units.la: 12 Climatibus terrae.) Alludit ad versus Hesiodi α. ὄμβρων[?], quos adscripsissem, nisi satis notos esse putarem.
units.tr: 12 With the climates of the earth.) He alludes to the verses of Hesiod, [ὄμβρων]. I would have cited them, but I think they are sufficiently well known.

units.la: 13 Cum hominis, omnisq; ratione praediti animalis.) Loquitur ex sententia philosophorum, qui λογικὸν ζῷον, animal ratione instructum, non soli homini, sed Deo etiam, daemonibus & heroibus genus constituerunt: de quo multa legi possunt hincinde apud Plutarch. praesertim vero
units.tr: 13 Of man, and of every animal endowed with reason.) He speaks in line with the philosophers who defined the rational animal [λογικὸν ζῷον] as a kind that includes not only man but also God, daemons and heroes. Much on this can be read here and there in Plutarch, especially

units.la: Quàm ut in terram utcunq; redigar.) Non enim tantum sacrae literae docent, hominem esse ex limo creatum, foreq; ut in eundem redigatur; sed & antiquissimi philosophi originem nostram eodem retulerunt. Hinc Prometheus dicitur e limo formasse hominem, de quo nullus no mentionem fecit poeta. Et apud Homerum Menelaus Graecis duellum contra Hectorem detrectatibus iratus, mortem eis ignobilem imprecatur his verbis,
units.tr: That I should be reduced somehow to earth. For not only do the sacred letters teach that man was created from clay and is destined to return to it, but also the most ancient philosophers traced our origin to the same source. Hence Prometheus is said to have formed man from clay, a thing no poet has mentioned. And in Homer, Menelaus, angry at the Greeks who shrank from fighting Hector, calls down an ignoble death upon them in these words:

units.la: ἀλλ' ὑμεῖς μὲν πάντες ὕδωρ τε γαῖα γένοισθε,
units.tr: [But may you all become water and earth.] [ἀλλ' ὑμεῖς μὲν πάντες ὕδωρ τε γαῖα γένοισθε]

units.la: Vos in aquam & terram cunctos convertier opto. Itaq; ἃ[?] hic tuli, neq; volui, quod poteram ad alium sensum cogitando diuertere.
units.tr: I wish that you all be turned into water and earth. So I have rendered it here as it stands, and did not wish to turn it to another sense by thinking, though I could.

units.la: Vide quid agant homines.) Queritur de iniquo hominum iudicio, qui cum aliis praesentibus laudem meritam testimoniumq; virtutis inuideant, ipsi ab ijs quos non viderunt, laudari volunt: cum nihil inde fructus possint ferre, iam ante mortui. Facit hoc egregie ad famam contemnendam.
units.tr: See what men do. He complains of the unjust judgment of men, who, while others are present, begrudge the deserved praise and the testimony of virtue, yet want to be praised by those they have never seen, when they can gain nothing from it, being already dead. This serves admirably to make one despise fame.

units.la: Non indignamur.) ὅτι ἐπισημαινόμεθα[?]. In malam partem usum vocabulo hoc, & ipse puto, & sententia testatur. Non recordor me apud vetustiores autores hoc vocabulum ita sumtum legisse. Appianus quidem Alexandrinus, haud ineruditus scriptor, eodem modo usurpavit lib. 5. ἐμφυλίων, de milite loquens, qui ludis in subsellia equitum ascen-derat. derat' ὁ Ἀ[?]ὐ[?]μ[?]ς ἐπεγνωμένα[?], ὡς ὁ Καῖσαρ τὴν πραπώτλυ ἀν[?]ὲ[?]σ[?]ηκ[?]σ[?]εν[?]: Populus murmure indignitatem rei testatus est, & Cæsar militem inde abduxit.
units.tr: We do not feel indignation. [ὅτι ἐπισημαινόμεθα.] That the word is used in a bad sense, both I myself think and the context shows. I do not recall having read this word taken in this way in older authors. Appian of Alexandria, a writer not without learning, did indeed use it in the same way in book 5, speaking of a soldier who had climbed onto the benches of the knights at the games: The people by murmuring showed their indignation at the affair, and Caesar led the soldier away from there.

units.la: 4 Inhumanum esse videtur.) Hic locus idē, sed paulo obscurius, videtur docere, quod Cicero ad Lentulum de Platonis sententia his verbis monet: Id enim iubet idem ille Plato, quem ego autorem vehementer sequor: Tantum contendere in republica, quantum probare civibus tuis possis: vim neq; parenti, neq; patriæ afferre oportere.
units.tr: 4 It seems inhuman. This passage seems to teach the same thing, though a little more obscurely, as Cicero, in his letter to Lentulus, admonishes concerning the opinion of Plato in these words: For that same Plato, whom I follow earnestly, bids this: strive in the state only as far as you can persuade your fellow citizens; one must not do violence either to parent or to fatherland.

units.la: 5 Vide ne à præsenti statu deiectus.) In Græco est, Ὅρα μὴ ἀποχωρισθῇς, μὴ βαφῇς: posterius est: Ne mergaris. Quid autem sit ἀποχωρισμὸς[?] (si, quod non iudico, Græcum est, aut omnino non depravatum vocabulum) nescio. Neq; vereor ne significet, imperio aut summa rerum deponi, ἀπὸ τ(οῦ) Καίσαρ[?]. neq; enim vel etymologia hæc auditu digna, vel sensus loci esset vllus, itaq; liberè mea verba supposui.
units.tr: 5 See that you are not cut off from your present condition. In the Greek it is: Ὅρα μὴ ἀποχωρισθῇς, μὴ βαφῇς. The later reading is: Ne mergaris (do not be plunged under). What ἀποχωρισμὸς means (if it is Greek, which I do not judge, or a word not corrupted at all) I do not know. Nor do I fear that it means being deposed from command or from the chief power, from the Caesar. For neither that etymology would be worth hearing, nor would the passage have any sense, and so I have freely supplied my own words.

units.la: 6 Antonini discipulum.) Pii scilicet, qui antecesserat eum in imperio.
units.tr: 6 Of Antoninus's disciple. Namely of Pius, who had preceded him in the empire.

units.la: 7 Quæ vultus serenitas.) τὸ ἀνόδιον τ[?] τρω[?] αὐτῆς[?]· legi ἀνδρῶν.
units.tr: 7 The serenity of countenance. The Greek reads τὸ ἀνόδιον…; I read ἀνδρῶν [andrōn].

units.la: 1 Velitationes.) In Græco est ἁλιλογατισμοί. Quod tamen vocabulum fateor me non satis intelligere. ἀόρυ[?] quidem hastam esse, vel pueri sciunt: item, ἀόγατ[?] esse eius patrium casum: ut ἀλιλογατισμὸς videatur esse hastiludium (quod barbari vocant) is est, concertatio hastis quædam inita. Sed haud scio quàm huc id quadret. Videtur autem, his omnibus humanæ vitæ vanitatem & varietatem voluisse demonstrare.
units.tr: 1 Skirmishes. In the Greek it is ἁλιλογατισμοί. Yet I confess I do not fully understand this word. Even boys know that ἀόρυ is a spear, and likewise that ἀόγατ is its genitive-type form in the paternal case; so that ἀλιλογατισμὸς seems to be the sport of spear-play (which the barbarians call hastiludium), that is, a kind of contest begun with spears. But I do not know how well this fits here. It seems, however, that by all these examples he wished to show the vanity and variety of human life.

units.la: Quàm multi quondam fuere.)Aliunde huic loco videntur hæc à librario esse intercalata: incommodè profectò, cùm alioquin sequentia optimè cum prioribus cohæreant, in quibus offendit, nonnunquam, vbi propriæ nos vires deficiunt, auxilium aliorum non aspernandum esse, dumodo nostrum officium faciamus. Etenim & Homericus ille Diomedes, socio adiuncto sperabat se propositum negotium rectius confecturum, vnde est illud Σὼ τε ἀὶ᾽ ὁρχομένω[?], vsitatum bonis autoribus, explicatumq; ab Aristotele libro 8. Ethicorum, de amicitia disputaturo.
units.tr: How many once there were. These sentences seem to have been inserted here by a copyist from somewhere else, which is certainly inappropriate, since otherwise what follows fits very well with what precedes, where it is noted that sometimes, when our own strength fails, the help of others is not to be spurned, provided we do our duty. For that Homeric Diomedes too, with a companion joined to him, hoped to carry out the proposed task more rightly; hence that saying [Σὼ τε ἀὶ᾽ ὁρχομένω], used by good authors and explained by Aristotle in book 8 of the Ethics, where he discusses friendship.

units.la: Membrum.)In Græco est μέλος, & pro parte μέρος. Porro non fallit eruditos, membrum respectu totius & reliquorum membrorum maiore deuinciri necessitate, quàm totius partes qualescunq;. Est enim omne membrum pars, non contrà. Multo ergo rectius societatem humanam & vniuersi coniunctionem intelligit, qui membrum se, quàm qui partem generis humani dicit. Discrimen hoc diuisionis εἰς μέλη & μέρη, etiam Strabo suæ rei accommodauit lib.2.
units.tr: Member. In Greek it is μέλος, and for part μέρος. Moreover, it is not unknown to scholars that a member, with respect to the whole and the other members, is bound by a greater necessity than the parts of a whole, whatever they may be. For every member is a part, but not conversely. Much more rightly, therefore, does he understand human society and the bond of the universe who calls himself a member than he who calls himself a part of the human race. Strabo too applied this distinction of division into μέλη and μέρη to his own subject in book 2.
Divine. Δαίμονες. It should be read Δαίμονες, or at least δαιμόνια.

units.la: Pauca secus.) ἡ ἀλλίαν[?]. lego ἡ ἀλὴ λίαν[?].Sunt autè passim per multa, in quibus ariolo magis quàm interprete opus sit.
units.tr: Somewhat otherwise. ἡ ἀλλίαν. I read ἡ ἀλὴ λίαν. There are moreover, scattered through many passages, places where one needs a guesser rather than an interpreter.

units.la: Nā rebus.)Promiscuè et mutilatè huc poetica quædā sunt congesta: partim infrà lib.XI. repetita.
units.tr: For in things. Poetic passages have been gathered here promiscuously and mutilated; some are repeated below in book XI.

units.la: Platonica ego .) Ex apologia Socratis hæc sunt.
units.tr: I, Platonic. These are from Socrates' Apology.

units.la: Credens ijs qui dicunt.) τῷ γυναικί[?], in Græco. Sanè Hector Homericus Iliad.ζ[?]. suam uxorem hac ipsa ratione consolatur, versu 487. Et est minimè muliebris hæc sententia, apud Poetas passim inculcata.
units.tr: Trusting those who say. τῷ γυναικί, in the Greek. Certainly Hector in Homer, Iliad 6, consoles his wife with this very reasoning, at verse 487. And this sentiment is by no means womanly; it is repeatedly inculcated among the poets.

units.la: Est aliquis te peritior.) Adnotatum est hoc loco à librario, nō esse hic novæ initium tractationis: sed cohærere cum his quæ ante ea quæ ex Platone sunt huc translata, præcedebant. Sed quia illa ipsa erant mutila, id quidem non video quale sit. καταβάλλων[?] lustratorem dici puto, παρὰ τὸ καταβάλλειν[?], deicere.
units.tr: There is someone more skilled than you. The copyist noted at this point that this is not the beginning of a new treatment, but coheres with what preceded those passages translated here from Plato. But since those passages were themselves mutilated, I do not see exactly what it is. I think καταβάλλων is said of a purifier (lustrator), from καταβάλλειν, to cast down.

units.la: Omnis animus, inquit ille.) Nimirum Plato in Protagora.
units.tr: Every soul, says he. Namely Plato, in the Protagoras.

units.la: Salaminium.) Leonem nomine, quem ad cædē ab eo duci Critias tyrannus volebat. vide Apologiam Socratis apud Platonem, & Diogene Laertium in vita Socratis.
units.tr: Salaminian. By name Leon, whom the tyrant Critias wanted to be led to death by him. See Plato's Apology of Socrates, and Diogenes Laertius in the Life of Socrates.

units.la: Pestis, bellum.) Pro pestis, in Græco est μίμ&Θ[?], minus quod non quadrare puto. sunt autem pleraq; lacera.
units.tr: Pestis, bellum.) For "pestis" the Greek has a word which I think does not fit well. Most of these readings are, moreover, corrupt.

units.la: 1 Expetit quidem.) Alludit adversus Euripideos, quorum metio est etiam apud Aristotelem initio octavi Moralium ad Nicomachum. Sunt autem, si quis dextre accipiat, quod hic fit, praeclari. Referit integros Athenaeus libro Δειπνοσοφ.[?] p. XIII.
units.tr: 1 Expetit quidem.) He alludes to the Euripideans, whose saying is also mentioned by Aristotle at the beginning of the eighth book of the Nicomachean Ethics. If one takes it rightly, as is done here, the sayings are excellent. Athenaeus reports them in full in book XIII of the Deipnosophists, p.

units.la: 1 Simplici obstinatione.) Ψιλὸν προτάξιν[?] ita verti, neq; tamen intelligo, cur hoc vel sic Christianis voluisset impingere crimen Antoninus, iam provecta ætate. qui quid aliis de iis scripserit, non est ignotum. Sed ista alio pertinent.
units.tr: 1 Simplici obstinatione.) I have translated the Greek phrase in this way, but I do not understand why Antoninus, now advanced in years, would have wished to impute this charge, or this kind of charge, to the Christians. What he wrote about them elsewhere is not unknown. But those matters belong elsewhere.

units.la: 2 Oportet igitur.) Divinare sum conatus. quod si sententia hæc fuit Antonini, certè est aurea, iis in rebus adhibita, in quibus pictas sinit.
units.tr: 2 Oportet igitur.) I have tried to guess at the meaning. If this was Antoninus' opinion, it is certainly golden, to be applied in those matters where circumstances allow.

units.la: 3 Insidiæ tectæ.) Σκαλμὸν. Mihi subit suspicari, σκαλλὼν legendum, schlimm. nam & Plutarch. obliquam & distortam viam σκαλμὸν ὁδὸν[?] alicubi vocat. Λυκοφιλίαι[?] quid sint, explicare adhuc non satis possum.
units.tr: 3 Insidiae tectae.) The word here is σκαλμόν. It occurs to me to suspect that σκαλλών should be read, "schlimm" (crooked). For Plutarch also calls a crooked and twisted path by this name somewhere. What the "Lykophiliai" are, I cannot yet explain adequately.
